Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.

This surah is Meccan. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah that "Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah" and "So be patient as the steadfast of the messengers were patient" (46:35) are two Medinan verses. The connection of its beginning with what precedes it is that at the end of what precedes it is: "That is because you took the signs of Allah in jest" (45:35), and you said that he (peace be upon him) invented it. So Allah the Exalted said: "Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise." These two attributes are the last of that and the first of this.

"And a specified term" means a appointed time for the ruin of this structure. Ibn ʿAbbas said it is the Resurrection; others said it means the term of every creature. "(From) what they are warned of": it may be that ma is a verbal (infinitive) particle, and it may be in the sense of "that which."

"Say: Have you considered those you call upon": its meaning is, tell me about those you call upon besides Allah, namely the idols.

"Show me what they have created from the earth": this is a question of rebuke. The first object of "Have you considered" is "those you call upon." "What they have created" is an interrogative clause that "Have you considered" requires, since its second object must be an interrogative; and "Show me" requires it by way of suspension (ta'liq). This is a case of iʿmal (operating the second of two verbs), the second verb operating and the second object of "Have you considered" being omitted. It is possible that "Show me" is an emphasis of "Have you considered," in the sense of "tell me," so that "Show me" means "inform me," as if both had one meaning.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "Have you considered" may have two possibilities. One is that it is transitive, with ma as its object. The other is that "Have you considered" is merely an alerting particle that does not take an object, and ma is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke, and "call upon" means "worship." End of quotation. That "Have you considered" is non-transitive and alerting has some difficulty; al-Akhfash said this about the verse, "He said: Have you seen, when we took refuge at the rock?" (18:63). What appears is that "what you call upon" is the object of "Have you considered," as it is in "Say: Have you considered your partners whom you call upon?" (35:40) in Surah Fatir, and the discussion of a parallel of this sentence was given there. The discussion of "Have you considered" has been fully treated in Surah al-An'am, so refer to it there. "From the earth" is an explanation of the vague "what they have created." The apparent meaning is that it means from parts of the earth, i.e., the creation of that is only for Allah; or it may be by omitting a modifier, i.e., from what is high upon the earth, that is, on its surface, of animals or otherwise. Then He made them stand over their statement and said: "Or": i.e., "rather."

"Or do they have a share in the heavens? Bring me a Book before this": i.e., before this Book, which is the Qur'an. The meaning is that this Qur'an speaks of monotheism and of the refutation of associating partners, and all of Allah's revealed books speak to that; so He demanded that they bring one single book that testifies to the soundness of what they hold of worshipping other than Allah.

"Or any trace of knowledge": i.e., a remnant of knowledge, that is, of the knowledge of the ancients, from the saying of them: "The she-camel grew fat on a trace of fat," or on a remnant of fat that remained on her from vanished fat. The word athara is used for a remnant of nobility; one says, "The sons of so-and-so have a trace of nobility," when they have ancient evidences. In other usage the poet al-Ra'i said: "And a she-camel with a trace ate for us a plant in its hillocks, dry lands," i.e., a remnant of fat. Al-Jumhur read "aw athāratin," which is a verbal noun like shaja'ah and samahah, and it is the remnant of a thing, as if it were a trace (athrah). Al-Hasan said the meaning is: knowledge you have extracted and then stir up. Mujahid said the meaning is: is there anyone who transmits knowledge concerning this? Al-Qurtubi said it is the chain of transmission, and from it is the saying of al-A'sha: "Indeed what you two disputed about has been made clear to the listener and the transmitter," i.e., and to those who seek other than it. From it is also the saying of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I left behind neither one who recounts nor one who transmits." Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman and Qatadah said the meaning is: or a special knowledge. Its derivation is from athara (preference), as if Allah had preferred those who possess it with it. Ibn ʿAbbas said the intended meaning of athara is a line in the dust, a thing the Arabs used to do, by which they practised divination and interpreted its omens. Writing with a line in the dust implies strengthening the matter of the line in the dust, and that it is a thing with no way to harm anyone who stands before it. It was said: if Ibn ʿAbbas's interpretation of athara as a line in the dust is sound, then it is of the nature of mockery toward them, their statements and their proofs. ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas (with a variant transmission from them), Zayd ibn ʿAli, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, al-Hasan, al-Sulami, al-Aʿmash and ʿAmr ibn Maymun read "aw athratin" without alif; it is singular, its plural being uthur, like qatarah and qutur. ʿAli, al-Sulami and Qatadah also read it with the thāʾ sukun, and it is the single act of what is transmitted, i.e., "I am content for you with a single report and a single transmission that testifies to the soundness of your saying." From al-Kisa'i: the hamza with damma and the thāʾ with sukun. Ibn Khalawayh said, and al-Kisa'i said in another dialect: ithrah and uthrah, meaning with the hamza kasra and damma.

﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah those who will not respond to him...﴾ refers to one who worships idols, which are inanimate and have no power to respond to their supplicants for as long as the world lasts. That is, they will never respond to them. For this reason, the negation of their responding is qualified by His words: "until the Day of Resurrection." Moreover, they have no awareness of being worshipped, and in the Hereafter they will be enemies to their worshippers. Thus there is no benefit to them from their worshippers in this world, and in the Hereafter they will be a source of harm to them, as the Exalted said: ﴿They will deny their worship of them, and they will be opposed to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. The phrase ﴿those who will not respond﴾ is used because the worshippers attribute to them what is attributed to people of knowledge, namely responding and paying attention. It seems that ﴿those who will not respond﴾ is intended to include whoever is worshipped besides Allah, whether human, jinn, or others, and the rational beings are given precedence. The pronoun was first returned to the wording of ﴿those who will not respond﴾, and then to its meaning in ﴿and they are﴾ that follows. The apparent reading is that the pronoun first returns to the wording of ﴿those who will not respond﴾, then to its meaning in "and they are" that follows, and it is in accordance with the meaning of "those" in ﴿those who will not respond﴾, as we have explained. It has also been said that it returns to the meaning of "who" in ﴿And who is more astray﴾, meaning: and the disbelievers, in their error, are those who call upon one who will not respond. (Heedless): they do not reflect upon the harm they bring upon themselves by calling upon one with such a description.

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear proofs﴾: "bayyinat" is the plural of "bayyina," which is the clear proof. The lam in "for the truth" (lil-haqq) is the lam of causation (lam al-ʿilla), meaning "on account of the truth." The speaker used the explicit nouns instead of the pronouns in ﴿Those who disbelieved say of the truth﴾, and did not use the construction "they say of it," to draw attention to two descriptions: the description of those to whom it is recited as disbelievers, and the description of what is recited to them as the truth. Had he used the pronouns for both descriptions, there would be no indication of the two descriptions from the standpoint of the wording, even though whoever named the verses "magic" is a disbeliever while the verses themselves are true. So, by mentioning both explicitly, it becomes impossible to attribute the description of disbelief to the speakers and the description of truth to what is recited. In his words "when it came to them" there is an alert that they did not reflect on what was recited to them; rather, at the first hearing they hastened to attribute it to magic, out of obstinacy and injustice, and they described it as "manifest" (mubin), that is, clear, meaning: it is magic with no doubt about it.

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ That is: rather they say, "He has invented it." That is, do they say he fabricated it? They moved from their saying ﴿This is magic﴾ to this other statement. The pronoun in "invented it" refers to the truth, and what is meant by it is the verses.

﴿Say: If I have invented it﴾, as a supposition, then Allah is sufficient for me in this matter. He is the One who would punish me for fabricating against Him and would not give me respite, so you would not be able to avert from me the punishment of Allah in any way. How, then, would I invent it and expose myself to His punishment? It is said: "So-and-so has no control when he is angry," and "He has no control over his rein when he is deaf." The eloquent and well-known usage is that "darā" takes the preposition bāʾ, and therefore when it is made transitive by the hamza of causation it takes bāʾ, as in His words: ﴿Nor would you have known it﴾ [Yunus: 16]. So making "ma" interrogative is the preferable and better reading, and often it is suspended in the Qur'an, as in: ﴿I do not know whether it is near﴾ [al-Anbiya: 109]. "Yuf'al" is affirmative, not negated, but the negation has extended to it because it is combined with "ma" and "yuf'al." Therefore He said: ﴿nor with you﴾. Were it not for considering the negation, the construction would be ﴿what will be done with me and with you﴾. Do you not see the insertion of "min" in His words: ﴿that any good should be sent down upon you﴾ [al-Baqara: 105]? It is because the negation of "those who disbelieved would not wish" [al-Baqara: 105] extends to "wish" and to the object of "wish," which is "that it be sent down." So when the desire for the sending down is negated, the sending down itself is negated. Ibn ʿUmayr read: "ma yuhi" with a kasra on the ha, meaning Allah, mighty and majestic.

(Say: Have you considered): the two objects of "Have you considered" are omitted, because the meaning indicates them. The estimated sense is: "Have you considered your state if it is so? Are you not wrongdoers?" So the first is "your state," and the second is "are you not wrongdoers." The answer to the condition is omitted, meaning: then you have wronged yourselves, and for this reason the verb of the condition is in the past tense. Al-Zamakhshari said: the answer to the condition is omitted, its estimated sense being: if this Qur'an is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, are you not wrongdoers? And this omitted part is indicated by His words: ﴿Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. End of quotation. But an interrogative clause cannot be an answer to a condition except with fa. If the particle is the hamza, the fa precedes it, as in: "If you visit us, do we not treat you well?" Or if it is another particle, the fa precedes it, as in: "If you visit us, do you see anything but good?" So al-Zamakhshari's "are you not wrongdoers?" without a fa cannot be the answer to the condition. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "Ara'aytum may be a particle of alerting, being a word set for asking that does not require an object. It may also be that the clause, 'it was' and what it governs, occupies the place of its two objects." End of quotation. This contradicts what the rigorous grammarians have established regarding ara'aytum. It has also been said: the answer to the condition is ....

﴿Then he believed while you were arrogant﴾: that is, Muhammad has indeed believed in it, or the witness, while you yourselves were arrogant toward belief. al-Hasan said: its estimated sense is: "then who is more astray than you?" It has also been said: "Who among us is rightly guided and who among you is in error?" It has also been said: "You are only destroying yourselves." The pronoun in "in it" returns to what the subject of "was" returns to, which is the Qur'an. al-Shaʿbi said it returns to the Messenger. The witness is ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, as stated by the majority, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, ʿIkrima, Mujahid, Qatada, and Ibn Sirin, and the verse is Medinan. It is reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam: "Verses of the Book of Allah were revealed concerning me: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like, and believed, while you were arrogant﴾." Masruq said: the witness is Musa, peace be upon him, not Ibn Salam, because he became Muslim in Medina, and the sura is Meccan. The address in ﴿and you disbelieved in it﴾ is to the Quraysh. al-Shaʿbi said: the witness is whoever among the Children of Israel believed in Musa and the Torah, because Ibn Salam became Muslim two years before the death of the Prophet ﷺ, and the sura is Meccan. Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, Mujahid, and a group said: the verse is Meccan, and the witness is ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, and it is one of the verses that contained an unseen matter that existence brought to light. ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam is mentioned in the Sahih, and in it is a refutation of the Jews, may Allah curse them.

Among the lies and ignorance of the Jews regarding history is what they believe about ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam: that when the Prophet ﷺ travelled to Syria on a trade mission for Khadija, may Allah be pleased with her, he met the rabbis of the Jews and related to them his dreams, and they understood that he was the possessor of a dominion, and they became blind, so they had ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam accompany him, and he learned the sciences and jurisprudence of the Torah for a period. They claimed, and exceeded in their lies, to the point that they attributed the miraculous eloquence found in the Qur'an to the composition of ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam. Yet this ʿAbd Allah is not known to have resided in Makka or to have frequented it. How much more of a liar and slanderer are the Jews, may Allah curse them! And consider what kind of group it is, for no group like them is condemned in the Qur'an.

Surah al-Ahqaf, thirty-five verses, Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

(p-53) Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth and for a specified term. But those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of. Say: "Have you considered those you call upon besides Allah? Show me what they have created from the earth, or do they have a share in the heavens? Bring me a Book before this, or any trace of knowledge, if you are truthful." And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, one who will not answer him until the Day of Resurrection, and who are heedless of their supplication? And when mankind is gathered, they will be enemies to them and will deny their worship. And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieve say of the truth when it comes to them, "This is obvious magic." Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"? Say: "If I have fabricated it, then you cannot avail me anything against Allah. He is most knowing of what you say about it. Sufficient is He as a witness between me and you, and He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." Say: "I am not a novelty among the messengers, and I do not know what will be done with me or with you. I only follow what is revealed to me, and I am only a clear warner." Say: "Have you considered: if this is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel testifies to its like and believes, while you are arrogant?" Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people. And those who disbelieve say of those who believe, "If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it." And since they were not guided by it, they will say, "This is an ancient falsehood."

(p-54) Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth and for a specified term. But those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of. Say: "Have you considered those you call upon besides Allah? Show me what they have created from the earth, or do they have a share in the heavens? Bring me a Book before this, or any trace of knowledge, if you are truthful." And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, one who will not answer him until the Day of Resurrection, and who are heedless of their supplication? And when mankind is gathered, they will be enemies to them and will deny their worship. And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieve say of the truth when it comes to them, "This is obvious magic." Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"? Say: "If I have fabricated it, then you cannot avail me anything against Allah. He is most knowing of what you say about it. Sufficient is He as a witness between me and you, and He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." Say: "I am not a novelty among the messengers, and I do not know what will be done with me or with you. I only follow what is revealed to me, and I am only a clear warner." Say: "Have you considered: if this is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel testifies to its like and believes, while you are arrogant?" Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.

This surah is Meccan. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah that "Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah" and "So be patient as the steadfast of the messengers were patient" (46:35) are two Medinan verses. The connection of its beginning with what precedes it is that at the end of what precedes it is: "That is because you took the signs of Allah in jest" (45:35), and you said that he (peace be upon him) invented it. So Allah the Exalted said: "Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise." These two attributes are the last of that and the first of this.

"And a specified term" means a appointed time for the ruin of this structure. Ibn ʿAbbas said it is the Resurrection; others said it means the term of every creature. "(From) what they are warned of": it may be that ma is a verbal (infinitive) particle, and it may be in the sense of "that which."

"Say: Have you considered those you call upon": its meaning is, tell me about those you call upon besides Allah, namely the idols.

"Show me what they have created from the earth": this is a question of rebuke. The first object of "Have you considered" is "those you call upon." "What they have created" is an interrogative clause that "Have you considered" requires, since its second object must be an interrogative; and "Show me" requires it by way of suspension (ta'liq). This is a case of iʿmal (operating the second of two verbs), the second verb operating and the second object of "Have you considered" being omitted. It is possible that "Show me" is an emphasis of "Have you considered," in the sense of "tell me," so that "Show me" means "inform me," as if both had one meaning.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "Have you considered" may have two possibilities. One is that it is transitive, with ma as its object. The other is that "Have you considered" is merely an alerting particle that does not take an object, and ma is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke, and "call upon" means "worship." End of quotation. That "Have you considered" is non-transitive and alerting has some difficulty; al-Akhfash said this about the verse, "He said: Have you seen, when we took refuge at the rock?" (18:63). What appears is that "what you call upon" is the object of "Have you considered," as it is in "Say: Have you considered your partners whom you call upon?" (35:40) in Surah Fatir, and the discussion of a parallel of this sentence was given there. The discussion of "Have you considered" has been fully treated in Surah al-An'am, so refer to it there. "From the earth" is an explanation of the vague "what they have created." The apparent meaning is that it means from parts of the earth, i.e., the creation of that is only for Allah; or it may be by omitting a modifier, i.e., from what is high upon the earth, that is, on its surface, of animals or otherwise. Then He made them stand over their statement and said: "Or": i.e., "rather."

"Or do they have a share in the heavens? Bring me a Book before this": i.e., before this Book, which is the Qur'an. The meaning is that this Qur'an speaks of monotheism and of the refutation of associating partners, and all of Allah's revealed books speak to that; so He demanded that they bring one single book that testifies to the soundness of what they hold of worshipping other than Allah.

"Or any trace of knowledge": i.e., a remnant of knowledge, that is, of the knowledge of the ancients, from the saying of them: "The she-camel grew fat on a trace of fat," or on a remnant of fat that remained on her from vanished fat. The word athara is used for a remnant of nobility; one says, "The sons of so-and-so have a trace of nobility," when they have ancient evidences. In other usage the poet al-Ra'i said: "And a she-camel with a trace ate for us a plant in its hillocks, dry lands," i.e., a remnant of fat. Al-Jumhur read "aw athāratin," which is a verbal noun like shaja'ah and samahah, and it is the remnant of a thing, as if it were a trace (athrah). Al-Hasan said the meaning is: knowledge you have extracted and then stir up. Mujahid said the meaning is: is there anyone who transmits knowledge concerning this? Al-Qurtubi said it is the chain of transmission, and from it is the saying of al-A'sha: "Indeed what you two disputed about has been made clear to the listener and the transmitter," i.e., and to those who seek other than it. From it is also the saying of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I left behind neither one who recounts nor one who transmits." Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman and Qatadah said the meaning is: or a special knowledge. Its derivation is from athara (preference), as if Allah had preferred those who possess it with it. Ibn ʿAbbas said the intended meaning of athara is a line in the dust, a thing the Arabs used to do, by which they practised divination and interpreted its omens. Writing with a line in the dust implies strengthening the matter of the line in the dust, and that it is a thing with no way to harm anyone who stands before it. It was said: if Ibn ʿAbbas's interpretation of athara as a line in the dust is sound, then it is of the nature of mockery toward them, their statements and their proofs. ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas (with a variant transmission from them), Zayd ibn ʿAli, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, al-Hasan, al-Sulami, al-Aʿmash and ʿAmr ibn Maymun read "aw athratin" without alif; it is singular, its plural being uthur, like qatarah and qutur. ʿAli, al-Sulami and Qatadah also read it with the thāʾ sukun, and it is the single act of what is transmitted, i.e., "I am content for you with a single report and a single transmission that testifies to the soundness of your saying." From al-Kisa'i: the hamza with damma and the thāʾ with sukun. Ibn Khalawayh said, and al-Kisa'i said in another dialect: ithrah and uthrah, meaning with the hamza kasra and damma.

﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah those who will not respond to him...﴾ refers to one who worships idols, which are inanimate and have no power to respond to their supplicants for as long as the world lasts. That is, they will never respond to them. For this reason, the negation of their responding is qualified by His words: "until the Day of Resurrection." Moreover, they have no awareness of being worshipped, and in the Hereafter they will be enemies to their worshippers. Thus there is no benefit to them from their worshippers in this world, and in the Hereafter they will be a source of harm to them, as the Exalted said: ﴿They will deny their worship of them, and they will be opposed to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. The phrase ﴿those who will not respond﴾ is used because the worshippers attribute to them what is attributed to people of knowledge, namely responding and paying attention. It seems that ﴿those who will not respond﴾ is intended to include whoever is worshipped besides Allah, whether human, jinn, or others, and the rational beings are given precedence. The pronoun was first returned to the wording of ﴿those who will not respond﴾, and then to its meaning in ﴿and they are﴾ that follows. The apparent reading is that the pronoun first returns to the wording of ﴿those who will not respond﴾, then to its meaning in "and they are" that follows, and it is in accordance with the meaning of "those" in ﴿those who will not respond﴾, as we have explained. It has also been said that it returns to the meaning of "who" in ﴿And who is more astray﴾, meaning: and the disbelievers, in their error, are those who call upon one who will not respond. (Heedless): they do not reflect upon the harm they bring upon themselves by calling upon one with such a description.

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear proofs﴾: "bayyinat" is the plural of "bayyina," which is the clear proof. The lam in "for the truth" (lil-haqq) is the lam of causation (lam al-ʿilla), meaning "on account of the truth." The speaker used the explicit nouns instead of the pronouns in ﴿Those who disbelieved say of the truth﴾, and did not use the construction "they say of it," to draw attention to two descriptions: the description of those to whom it is recited as disbelievers, and the description of what is recited to them as the truth. Had he used the pronouns for both descriptions, there would be no indication of the two descriptions from the standpoint of the wording, even though whoever named the verses "magic" is a disbeliever while the verses themselves are true. So, by mentioning both explicitly, it becomes impossible to attribute the description of disbelief to the speakers and the description of truth to what is recited. In his words "when it came to them" there is an alert that they did not reflect on what was recited to them; rather, at the first hearing they hastened to attribute it to magic, out of obstinacy and injustice, and they described it as "manifest" (mubin), that is, clear, meaning: it is magic with no doubt about it.

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ That is: rather they say, "He has invented it." That is, do they say he fabricated it? They moved from their saying ﴿This is magic﴾ to this other statement. The pronoun in "invented it" refers to the truth, and what is meant by it is the verses.

﴿Say: If I have invented it﴾, as a supposition, then Allah is sufficient for me in this matter. He is the One who would punish me for fabricating against Him and would not give me respite, so you would not be able to avert from me the punishment of Allah in any way. How, then, would I invent it and expose myself to His punishment? It is said: "So-and-so has no control when he is angry," and "He has no control over his rein when he is deaf." A similar usage is: ﴿Who could prevent Allah from anything if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 17] and ﴿Whoever Allah intends to test, you cannot avail him anything against Allah﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 41]. From the same usage is his statement, upon him be blessings and peace: "I have no control for you against Allah in anything." Then he submitted himself to Allah and sought His help, saying: ﴿He knows best what you plunge into﴾: that is, what you rush into of falsehood, while what he means is the truth, and naming it at times "magic" and at times "slander." The pronoun in "into it" may refer to "what" or to the Qur'an, and "with Him" in the position of the subject suffices as a witness according to the most correct opinions.

﴿A witness between me and you﴾: a witness for me of conveying the message and calling to Him, and a witness against you of denial. (And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful): a promise to them of forgiveness and mercy if they turn back from disbelief, and an indication of His forbearance towards them, since He did not hasten to punish them, given that what preceded was a threat to them that He would hasten their punishment for their disbelief.

﴿Say: I am not something new among the messengers﴾: that is, others came before me. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada. The words bidʿ and badiʿ refer to things of which the like has not been seen before. From this is the verse of ʿAdi ibn Zayd, which Qutrub recited:

"I am no novelty among the events that befall
men, who were made happy after my misery."

Bidʿ and badiʿ are like khiff and khafif. Bidʿa is that which is invented and did not exist before. "The poet abdaʿa" means he brought something novel. "Shayʾun bidʿ," with a kasra, means something innovated. "So-and-so is bidʿ in this matter," meaning he is unique in it. The plural is abdaʿ, according to al-Akhfash. ʿIkrima, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with a fatha on the dal, as the plural of bidʿa, and this is by omitting a noun, meaning "possessors of novelties." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be an adjective on the pattern fiʿal, as they say: dinun qiyam and lahmun ziyam." End of quotation. As for what he permitted here, if its usage is not reported from the Arabs we do not permit it, because Sibawayh did not transmit from the pattern fiʿal in adjectives except ʿidan. Sibawayh said: "We do not know it to occur as an adjective except in a weak-radical word describing the plural, which is qawmun ʿidan." He later corrected himself, and his correction is sound. As for qiyam, its origin is qiyam, and qiyam is a shortened form of it, which is why the waw in it is weak; had it not been shortened, it would have remained sound, as in ḥiwal and ʿiwaḍ. As for the Arabs' sayings: makanun siwan, māʾun riwan, rajulun riḍan, māʾun ṣiran, and sabyun ṭiyaba, they are interpreted by the Basrans, who do not use them to establish the pattern fiʿal in adjectives. It is reported from Mujahid and Abu Haywa: bidaʿan, with a fatha on the ba and a kasra on the dal, like ḥadhar.

﴿I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾: that is, regarding what will come in time. That is, I do not know what is decreed for me and for you of His decrees, since His actions, may He be exalted, are known only to Him. It is reported from al-Hasan and a group: "I do not know what my affair and your affair will become in this world, and who among us will be the victor and who the vanquished." It is reported from al-Kalbi that his companions said to him, when they had grown weary of the harm of the polytheists: "How long must we remain in this state?" He said: "I do not know what will be done with me or with you. Will I descend in Makka, or will I be commanded to leave for a land that I have seen raised, meaning in a dream, with date palms and trees?" Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas ibn Malik, Qatada, al-Hasan, and ʿIkrima said: its meaning is in the Hereafter, and this was in the early period of Islam. Then afterward Allah, may He be exalted, made known to him that He had forgiven him what preceded of his sin and what followed, and that the believers have from Allah great grace, which is Paradise, and that the disbelievers are in the fire of Hell. This view is not apparent, rather He, glorified is He, had made known from the very beginning of the prophethood the state of the disbeliever and the state of the believer. It has been said: "what will be done with me or with you" refers to commands and prohibitions and what the Law requires. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning a matter that the Prophet ﷺ was awaiting from Allah, other than reward and punishment.

﴿I follow only what is revealed to me﴾: a submission and a disclaimer of knowledge of the unseen, and a restriction to warning alone, except from the punishment of Allah. The majority read "yuf'al" with a damma on the ya, in the passive voice, while Zayd ibn ʿAli and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with a fatha. The apparent view is that "ma" is interrogative and "adri" is suspended, so the interrogative clause is in the position of an object clause in the accusative. End of quotation. Were it not for considering the negation, the construction would be ﴿what will be done with me and with you﴾. So when the desire for the sending down is negated, the sending down itself is negated. Ibn ʿUmayr read: "ma yuhi" with a kasra on the ha, meaning Allah, mighty and majestic.

Or if it is another particle, the fa precedes it, as in: "If you visit us, do you see anything but good?" ﴿Then he believed while you were arrogant﴾: that is, Muhammad has indeed believed in it, or the witness, while you yourselves were arrogant toward belief. al-Hasan said: its estimated sense is: "then who is more astray than you?" It has also been said: "Who among us is rightly guided and who among you is in error?" It has also been said: "You are only destroying yourselves." Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 46, verses 11–19 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it. And since they are not guided by it, they will say, 'This is an ancient falsehood.'"﴾ ﴿And before it was the Book of Moses, a guide and a mercy. And this is a Book confirming it in the Arabic tongue, to warn those who wronged, and as good tidings for the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise, abiding therein, as a reward for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents.﴾ ﴿His mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship, and his carrying and weaning is thirty months, until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years, he says, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that pleases You. And make righteous for me my offspring. Indeed, I have repented to You, and indeed I am of the Muslims."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones from whom We accept the best of what they did and overlook their misdeeds, among the companions of Paradise, a true promise which they were promised.﴾ ﴿And the one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both! Do you promise me that I will be brought forth when generations have passed before me?" While they both call upon Allah for help, "Woe to you! Believe, for indeed the promise of Allah is true." But he says, "This is nothing but the fables of the former peoples."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones against whom the word has come into effect, among nations that passed away before them of jinn and mankind. Indeed, they were losers.﴾ ﴿And for all there are degrees according to what they did, and that He may fully repay them their deeds, and they will not be wronged.﴾.

[p. 59] Qatadah said: This is the statement of the disbelievers of Quraysh to those who believed, meaning: for the sake of those who believed. The lam is for communication (tabligh). Then they shifted to the third person in their saying ﴿ma sabaquna﴾ (they did not precede us). Had they not shifted, the speech would have been "ma sabaqtum ilayhi" (you did not precede us to it). When they heard that a group had believed, they addressed a group of the believers, that is, they said ﴿to those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it"﴾: those whose faith had reached them, meaning ʿAmmar, Suhayb, Bilal and others like them from among those who embraced Islam and believed in the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj said: this is the statement of Kinanah, ʿAmir and the rest of the neighboring Arab tribes. They said this when Ghifar, Muzaynah and Juhaynah embraced Islam, meaning: had this religion been good, the herdsmen would not have preceded us to it. Al-Tha'labi said: it is the statement of the Jews when Ibn Salam and others among them embraced Islam. Abu al-Mutawakkil said: Abu Dharr embraced Islam, then Ghifar embraced Islam, and Quraysh said this. It was also said: a slave-woman of ʿUmar embraced Islam, and he used to beat her until he tired, and he would say, "Were it not that I have tired, I would have increased your beating." The disbelievers of Quraysh then said: had what Muhammad calls to been true, this woman would not have preceded us to it. The apparent meaning is that the subject of kana (was) is the Qur'an, and the pronoun in bihi (to it) refers back to it and is supported by ﴿And before it was the Book of Moses﴾. It was also said that the pronoun in bihi refers to the Messenger, and the governing element of idh (when) is omitted, meaning ﴿and since they are not guided by it﴾, their obstinacy became manifest. His saying "fasa-yaqulun" (so they will say) is a consequence of that omitted answer, because this statement arises from obstinacy. It is impossible for fa-sa-yaqulun to govern idh, due to the intervening fa and the conflict between the time of idh and the time of sa-yaqulun.

﴿ifkun qadim﴾ (an ancient falsehood), just as they said: ﴿fables of the former peoples﴾. Its antiquity is due to the passage of ages over it.

When they attacked the soundness of the Qur'an, it was said to them: Allah sent down the Torah to Moses before it, and you do not dispute this, so the sending down of the Qur'an should not be disputed either. (imaman) means "one who is guided by it." Indeed, in it there is good news of the sending and mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so it is necessary to follow him and believe in him. Imaman is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and its governing element is the governing element of ﴿wa-min qablihi﴾, meaning: and the Book of Moses was before the Qur'an in the state of being a guide. Al-Kalbi recited "kitaba Musa" with a nasb and a fath on the mim of man, taking it as a relative pronoun, its estimated meaning being: and We gave him who came before it the Book of Moses. It was also said: imaman is accusative by an omitted element, meaning: We sent it down as an imam, that is, a model to be followed, and (rahmatan) is a mercy for whoever acts upon it. "This" refers to the Qur'an.

﴿A Book confirming﴾ it, meaning confirming the Book of Moses, which is the Torah, which contained its report and the report of the one who brought it, namely the Messenger. So he came confirming those reports, or confirming the divine Books. As for lisanan (in the tongue), it is a state (hal) from the pronoun in "musaddiq" (confirming), and its governing element is musaddiq, or it is from "kitab," since the governing element in it has described the demonstrative noun. Or lisanan is a state of its position (mawti'uhu), and the real state is "arabiyyan" (Arabic). Or it is in the sense of "one whose matter is Arabic," in which case it is an object of musaddiq, meaning this Qur'an confirms the one who brought it, who is the Messenger, and that is by its inimitability and its eloquent conditions. It was also said: it is accusative by dropping the preposition, meaning "in an Arabic tongue." Abu Raja', Shayba, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Ibn ʿAmir, Nafi' and Ibn Kathir recited "li-tundhira" with the second-person address to the Messenger, while al-A'mash, Ibn Kathir also, and the rest of the seven read it with the third-person yā' (li-yundhira), meaning: the Qur'an warns us. "Those who wronged" are the disbelievers who worship idols, in that they placed worship in other than the one who deserves it.

﴿And good tidings﴾: it was said it is coordinated with "musaddiq" and thus in the nominative position, or by an implied huwa (it). It was also said it is accusative by an omitted verb coordinated with li-yundhira, meaning: and to give good tidings, good tidings. It was also said it is accusative by dropping the preposition, meaning: and for good tidings. Al-Zamakhshari, and Abu al-Baqa' following him, said: and bushra is in the accusative position, coordinated with the position of li-yundhira, because it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). This is not permissible according to the sound view of the grammarians' school, because they stipulate for coordinating with the position that the position must be by original right (haqq al-asalah), and that there must be a place for it to be located. The position here is not by original right, because the original is the genitive for the maf'ul lahu, and the accusative arises from dropping the preposition. But when this occurred under the conditions mentioned in grammar, the verb reached it and governed it in the accusative. When He spoke of the disbelievers as "those who wronged," He spoke of the believers as "the doers of good," so that the word for good would be contrasted with the word for wrong.

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast﴾: the discussion of this verse's counterpart has preceded in surah Fussilat. When He mentioned ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾, He said "And We have enjoined," since kindness to the parents is the second-best of deeds, as in the sound report: "Which deed is best?" He said: "Prayer at its appointed time." He said: "Then which?" He said: "Then kindness to one's parents." Although their disobedience is the second greatest of the major sins, as the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins? Associating partners with Allah and disobedience to one's parents." The reports on kindness to them are many.

The majority recited ḥusnan with a damma on the ḥa and sukun on the sin. ʿAli, al-Sulami and ʿIsa recited it with fatha on both. From ʿIsa also: with damma on both. The Kufans recited iḥsanan. It was said: wa-wassayna is taken to imply "alzamna" (We obligated), which is transitive to two objects, so ḥusnan and iḥsanan are in the accusative as the second object of wa-wassayna. It was also said the meaning is: an enjoining of one who is good, or of one who does good. It is possible that ḥusnan means iḥsan, in which case it is an object of purpose, meaning: We enjoined him concerning them out of Our kindness to them, so the kindness is from Allah, exalted is He. It was also said the accusative is an infinitive (maṣdar) by making wa-wassayna imply "aḥsanna" (We did good), by enjoining upon man concerning his parents an act of kindness. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: and the accusative of this, meaning iḥsanan, is a plain infinitive and the second object of the genitive term, and the bāʾ is connected to wa-wassayna or to his saying iḥsanan. End of quote. It is not correct that it is connected to iḥsanan, because it is preceded by a verbal particle of the infinitive, and so its complement cannot precede it. Also, aḥsana is not transitive by the bāʾ; it is transitive by the lām. You say "aḥsantu li-Zaydin" (I did good to Zayd), and you do not say "aḥsantu bi-Zaydin," in the sense that the kindness reaches him. The discussion of ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 8] has preceded in surah al-ʿAnkabut, and it has been brought here with the discussion of that, as an additional benefit.

﴿His mother carried him with hardship﴾: the hardship is not at the beginning of her conception, but in the continuation of the pregnancy, since she has no control over carrying him or leaving him. End of quote. It is not that hardship befalls her at that time, so this is a remote possibility. Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the meaning is that she carried him with difficulty and gave birth to him with difficulty. The majority recited kurhan with a damma on the kaf. Shayba, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, the two Haramis (Makkan and Madinan) and Abu ʿAmr recited it with fatha. Abu Raja', Mujahid and ʿIsa recited it with both. The damma and fatha are two dialects with one meaning, like al-ʿaqr and al-ʿuqr. A group said: with damma it means hardship, and with fatha it means compulsion and coercion. They weakened the fatha recitation. Some said: if it were with fatha, she would have to be forced against herself, since its meaning is coercion and overpowering. End of quote. This is nothing, since the fatha recitation is in the seven mutawatir (widely transmitted) readings. Abu Hatim said: the recitation with fatha on the kaf is not good, because kurh with fatha means compulsion and overpowering. End of quote. Abu Hatim used to criticize some of the Qur'an with what he had no knowledge of, out of audacity on his part, may Allah pardon him. Their being in the accusative as states from the subject pronoun means: she carried him in a state of hardship, or it is an adjective of an omitted infinitive, meaning: a carrying that is hard.

﴿And his carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾: that is, the period of his carrying and weaning. This can only be if one of the two ends is shortened, either by the woman giving birth after six months and nursing for two years, or by her giving birth after nine months according to custom and nursing for two years minus a quarter of a year. If the gestation period increases, the period of nursing decreases. So the nursing period is one year and nine months, and completing the two years is for whoever wishes to complete the nursing. Experience has revealed that the minimum gestation period is six months, as the text of the Qur'an states. Galen said: I investigated diligently the usual duration of pregnancy, and I saw a woman who gave birth after one hundred and eighty-four nights. Ibn Sina claimed that he witnessed this. As for the maximum length of pregnancy, there is nothing in the Qur'an that indicates it. Ibn Sina said in al-Shifa': It reached me from someone I trust completely that a woman gave birth after the fourth year of pregnancy, and the child she bore had teeth growing. It is related from Aristotle that he said: the gestation period for every animal is fixed except for man, so it may happen that a child is born after seven months or eight, and rarely does the child survive in the eighth month, except in certain lands such as Egypt. End of quote. He expressed nursing by "fisal" (weaning) because nursing follows weaning and is connected to it, since it ends with it and is completed by it, so it was named after it. The majority recited wa-fisaluhu, which is the verbal noun of fasala, as if it is from two parties: he separated from his mother and she separated from him. Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Jahdari recited wa-faslahu. It was said that fasl and fisal are both verbal nouns, like fatm and fitam (weaning). Here is a subtle point: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the mother three times in His saying "to his parents," and in carrying him and nursing him, which is expressed by weaning, and He mentioned the father once in His saying "to his parents." This accords with what the Messenger said about making three-quarters of righteousness for the mother and one-quarter for the father: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, who deserves my goodness most?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your father.'"

﴿Until, when he reaches his maturity﴾: there is an omission in the speech, which would be: "until" as a limit for it, its estimated meaning: then he lived after that, or his life continued. The discussion of ﴿reaches his maturity﴾ has preceded in surah Yusuf. The apparent meaning is that the view of the one who says that reaching maturity is forty is weak, because of the conjunction ﴿and reaches forty years﴾. Conjunction requires difference, unless it is claimed that this is an emphasis on reaching maturity, in which case it is possible; but establishing a new meaning is preferable to emphasis. Reaching forty is the completion of reason, since the signs of success appear. It was said: no prophet was sent except after forty. It is said in a hadith: "Indeed, Satan drags his hand over the face of one who exceeds forty and does not repent, and says: 'By my father, a face that will not prosper!'"

﴿He said: "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that pleases You﴾: The discussion of this has preceded in surah al-Naml.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 46, verse 11–19 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And make my offspring righteous for me﴾: He asked that his offspring be made a place for righteousness and a likely source of it, as if he had said: "Grant me righteousness in my offspring," and so He placed it in them. Or it is implied (dammana): "And be kind to me in my offspring" (wa-ṭuff bī fī dhurriyyatī), because aṣlaḥ (to make righteous) takes a direct object by itself, as in His saying: ﴿And We made righteous for him his wife﴾ [al-Anbiya': 90]; therefore the phrase ﴿in my offspring﴾ needed interpretation. It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), and it extends to those after him. This is problematic, because it was revealed in Mecca, and his father embraced Islam in the year of the Conquest. And as for His saying: ﴿Those are they from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾: by this is not meant Abu Bakr or anyone else. The intended sense of "man" (al-insan) is the species, and therefore He indicated with His saying "those" (ulā'ika) in the plural. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yutaqabbalu" in the passive voice, with "aḥsanu" in the nominative, and likewise "wa-yatajawwazu"; Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Abu Ja'far, and al-A'mash (with a variant from him) read thus too. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read "nataqabbalu" with "aḥsana" in the accusative, and "natajawwazu" with the nun in both; al-Hasan, al-A'mash, and 'Isa read with the ya' in both, fathah, and "aḥsana" in the accusative.

﴿Among the companions of the Garden﴾: it was said that fi (in) here means ma'a (with). It was also said that it is like your saying: "The Amir honored me among a group of his companions," meaning among the total of those he honored from among them. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), in the sense of "being among the companions of the Garden." The phrase ﴿a true promise﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the preceding sentence, because His saying ﴿Those are they whom We accept﴾ is a promise from Him, may He be exalted, of acceptance and forgiveness. When He mentioned the person who was dutiful to his parents and what good resulted for him, He mentioned the one who was undutiful to his parents and what evil resulted for him. The intended sense of "those who" (alladhī) is the species, and therefore the predicate came in the plural in His saying: ﴿Those are they against whom the Word has come into effect﴾. Al-Hasan said: it refers to the disbelieving, undutiful son who denies resurrection. As for the saying of Marwan ibn al-Hakam, followed by Qatadah, that it was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, it is an erroneous statement arising from injustice, when Marwan, who was governor of Madinah, called for the allegiance to Yazid. 'Abd al-Rahman said: "Have you made it Heraclian (Hirqliyyah)? Whenever Heraclius dies, his son succeeds, and whenever Caesar dies, his son succeeds?" Marwan said: "Seize him!" So he entered the house of his sister 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), and 'A'ishah denied that. She said, and she was the one of truthful report (al-mastudaqah): "No verse of the Qur'an was revealed concerning the family of Abu Bakr except my innocence." She said: "By Allah, it is not about him, and if I wished to name him, I would have named him." She turned Marwan away and said: "But Allah cursed your father while you were in his loins, so you are a fragment (fadaḍ) of the curse of Allah." What proves the corruption of this statement is that He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Those are they against whom the Word has come into effect﴾, and these are the attributes of the disbelievers, the people of the Fire; and 'Abd al-Rahman was among the most excellent of the Companions, their chiefs and their heroes, and among those who had a notable contribution to Islam on the Day of Yamamah and other occasions.

﴿Uff to you both﴾: The discussion of uff, its meaning, dialects, and reading has preceded in Surah al-Isra'. The lam in "lakumā" is for explanation, i.e., for you both, I mean the expression of annoyance (ta'fif). The majority read ﴿Do you promise me﴾ with two nuns, the first kasrah; al-Hasan, 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr, and in one narration Hisham, read with the assimilation of the nun of the nominative into the nun of protection (nūn al-wiqāyah). Nafi' in one narration and a group read with a single nun. al-Hasan, Shaybah, and Abu Ja'far, with a variant from him, and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr, and Harun ibn Musa from al-Jahdari, and Sam from Hisham read with fathah on the first nun, as if they fled from the two kasrahs and the ya' toward fathah seeking lightness, so they made it fathah, just as the one who assimilates and the one who deletes fled. Abu Hatim said: fathah on the nun is false, an error.

(That I be brought forth): i.e., that I be brought out from my grave for resurrection and reckoning. The majority read "an ukhraja" in the passive voice, while al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, al-A'mash, Ibn Musarrif, and al-Dahhak read it in the active voice.

﴿And generations had passed away before me﴾: i.e., they had passed on, and none of them was brought out or resurrected. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: ﴿And generations had passed away before me﴾ denying resurrection.

﴿While both of them call upon Allah for help﴾: it is said: istaghath Allah and istaghath bi-Allah, and both usages are in the Arabic language. We have already refuted Ibn Malik's denial of its transitivity with the bā', and we mentioned evidence for that in al-Anfal. That is, they say: "Help (al-ghiyath) is with Allah from you and from your saying," and it is an exaggeration of his statement.

﴿Woe to you﴾: an invocation against him for destruction, and what is meant by it is urging and encouraging toward faith, not the literal reality of perdition. It was said: woe to you is said to one who is belittled and provoked toward a matter he is hastening toward. The Arab reader al-A'raj and 'Amr ibn Fa'idah read ﴿That the promise of Allah﴾ with fathah on the hamzah, i.e., "believe that the promise of Allah is true"; the majority read it with kasrah. ﴿And he says: "What is this?"﴾: i.e., what is this that he says? i.e., about the promise of resurrection from graves, "is nothing but tales of the ancients, which they wrote down in their books," and there is no reality to it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent sense of the words of this verse is that it was revealed concerning a specific individual who was spoken to and said such things, and Allah refuted his statements as a warning against falling into their like.

His saying "those" (ulā'ika), its apparent sense is that it is an indication of a species included in His saying "and the one who says," and it is possible that the verse concerns a specific individual, and His saying "those" would mean the category and species of this mentioned one: ﴿those against whom the Word has come into effect﴾, i.e., the word of Allah that He will punish them, ﴿among nations that had passed away before them of jinn and men﴾, meaning the totality of nations. This indicates that the jinn die generation after generation like men. al-Hasan said in one of his gatherings: the jinn do not die; Qatadah objected to him with this verse, and he fell silent. al-'Abbas, from Abu 'Amr, read ﴿that they were﴾ with fathah on the hamzah, and the majority with kasrah.

﴿And for each are degrees﴾: i.e., of the good-doer and the evil-doer, ﴿degrees﴾ — the term "degrees" (darajat) predominates, since Paradise consists of degrees (darajat) and the Fire of levels (darakat). The meaning: ranks and stations of reward for what they did of good and evil, and because of what they did of them. Ibn Zayd said: the degrees of the good-doers ascend upward, and the degrees of the evil-doers descend downward. End. The one providing the reason is omitted; its estimate is: "and that He may fully pay them their deeds in the measure of their recompense," so reward was made degrees and punishment was made levels. The majority read ﴿and that He may fully pay them﴾ with the ya', i.e., Allah, may He be exalted; al-A'mash, al-A'raj, Shaybah, Abu Ja'far, the two brothers, Ibn Dhakwan, and Nafi' (with a variant from him) read it with the nun; and al-Sulami read it with the ta' from above, i.e., "and We will fully pay them the degrees," attributing the fulfillment to them metaphorically.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 46, verses 11–19 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it. And since they are not guided by it, they will say, 'This is an ancient falsehood.'"﴾ ﴿And before it was the Book of Moses, a guide and a mercy. And this is a Book confirming it in the Arabic tongue, to warn those who wronged, and as good tidings for the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise, abiding therein, as a reward for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents.﴾ ﴿His mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship, and his carrying and weaning is thirty months, until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years, he says, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that pleases You. And make righteous for me my offspring. Indeed, I have repented to You, and indeed I am of the Muslims."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones from whom We accept the best of what they did and overlook their misdeeds, among the companions of Paradise, a true promise which they were promised.﴾ ﴿And the one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both! Do you promise me that I will be brought forth when generations have passed before me?" While they both call upon Allah for help, "Woe to you! Believe, for indeed the promise of Allah is true." But he says, "This is nothing but the fables of the former peoples."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones against whom the word has come into effect, among nations that passed away before them of jinn and mankind. Indeed, they were losers.﴾ ﴿And for all there are degrees according to what they did, and that He may fully repay them their deeds, and they will not be wronged.﴾.

[p. 59] Qatadah said: This is the statement of the disbelievers of Quraysh to those who believed, meaning: for the sake of those who believed. The lam is for communication (tabligh). Then they shifted to the third person in their saying ﴿ma sabaquna﴾ (they did not precede us). Had they not shifted, the speech would have been "ma sabaqtum ilayhi" (you did not precede us to it). When they heard that a group had believed, they addressed a group of the believers, that is, they said ﴿to those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it"﴾: those whose faith had reached them, meaning ʿAmmar, Suhayb, Bilal and others like them from among those who embraced Islam and believed in the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj said: this is the statement of Kinanah, ʿAmir and the rest of the neighboring Arab tribes. They said this when Ghifar, Muzaynah and Juhaynah embraced Islam, meaning: had this religion been good, the herdsmen would not have preceded us to it. Al-Tha'labi said: it is the statement of the Jews when Ibn Salam and others among them embraced Islam. Abu al-Mutawakkil said: Abu Dharr embraced Islam, then Ghifar embraced Islam, and Quraysh said this. It was also said: a slave-woman of ʿUmar embraced Islam, and he used to beat her until he tired, and he would say, "Were it not that I have tired, I would have increased your beating." The disbelievers of Quraysh then said: had what Muhammad calls to been true, this woman would not have preceded us to it. The apparent meaning is that the subject of kana (was) is the Qur'an, and the pronoun in bihi (to it) refers back to it and is supported by ﴿And before it was the Book of Moses﴾. It was also said that the pronoun in bihi refers to the Messenger, and the governing element of idh (when) is omitted, meaning ﴿and since they are not guided by it﴾, their obstinacy became manifest. His saying "fasa-yaqulun" (so they will say) is a consequence of that omitted answer, because this statement arises from obstinacy. It is impossible for fa-sa-yaqulun to govern idh, due to the intervening fa and the conflict between the time of idh and the time of sa-yaqulun.

﴿ifkun qadim﴾ (an ancient falsehood), just as they said: ﴿fables of the former peoples﴾. Its antiquity is due to the passage of ages over it.

When they attacked the soundness of the Qur'an, it was said to them: Allah sent down the Torah to Moses before it, and you do not dispute this, so the sending down of the Qur'an should not be disputed either. (imaman) means "one who is guided by it." Indeed, in it there is good news of the sending and mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so it is necessary to follow him and believe in him. Imaman is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and its governing element is the governing element of ﴿wa-min qablihi﴾, meaning: and the Book of Moses was before the Qur'an in the state of being a guide. Al-Kalbi recited "kitaba Musa" with a nasb and a fath on the mim of man, taking it as a relative pronoun, its estimated meaning being: and We gave him who came before it the Book of Moses. It was also said: imaman is accusative by an omitted element, meaning: We sent it down as an imam, that is, a model to be followed, and (rahmatan) is a mercy for whoever acts upon it. "This" refers to the Qur'an.

﴿A Book confirming﴾ it, meaning confirming the Book of Moses, which is the Torah, which contained its report and the report of the one who brought it, namely the Messenger. So he came confirming those reports, or confirming the divine Books. As for lisanan (in the tongue), it is a state (hal) from the pronoun in "musaddiq" (confirming), and its governing element is musaddiq, or it is from "kitab," since the governing element in it has described the demonstrative noun. Or lisanan is a state of its position (mawti'uhu), and the real state is "arabiyyan" (Arabic). Or it is in the sense of "one whose matter is Arabic," in which case it is an object of musaddiq, meaning this Qur'an confirms the one who brought it, who is the Messenger, and that is by its inimitability and its eloquent conditions. It was also said: it is accusative by dropping the preposition, meaning "in an Arabic tongue." Abu Raja', Shayba, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Ibn ʿAmir, Nafi' and Ibn Kathir recited "li-tundhira" with the second-person address to the Messenger, while al-A'mash, Ibn Kathir also, and the rest of the seven read it with the third-person yā' (li-yundhira), meaning: the Qur'an warns us. "Those who wronged" are the disbelievers who worship idols, in that they placed worship in other than the one who deserves it.

﴿And good tidings﴾: it was said it is coordinated with "musaddiq" and thus in the nominative position, or by an implied huwa (it). It was also said it is accusative by an omitted verb coordinated with li-yundhira, meaning: and to give good tidings, good tidings. It was also said it is accusative by dropping the preposition, meaning: and for good tidings. Al-Zamakhshari, and Abu al-Baqa' following him, said: and bushra is in the accusative position, coordinated with the position of li-yundhira, because it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). This is not permissible according to the sound view of the grammarians' school, because they stipulate for coordinating with the position that the position must be by original right (haqq al-asalah), and that there must be a place for it to be located. The position here is not by original right, because the original is the genitive for the maf'ul lahu, and the accusative arises from dropping the preposition. But when this occurred under the conditions mentioned in grammar, the verb reached it and governed it in the accusative. When He spoke of the disbelievers as "those who wronged," He spoke of the believers as "the doers of good," so that the word for good would be contrasted with the word for wrong.

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast﴾: the discussion of this verse's counterpart has preceded in surah Fussilat. When He mentioned ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾, He said "And We have enjoined," since kindness to the parents is the second-best of deeds, as in the sound report: "Which deed is best?" He said: "Prayer at its appointed time." He said: "Then which?" He said: "Then kindness to one's parents." Although their disobedience is the second greatest of the major sins, as the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins? Associating partners with Allah and disobedience to one's parents." The reports on kindness to them are many.

The majority recited ḥusnan with a damma on the ḥa and sukun on the sin. ʿAli, al-Sulami and ʿIsa recited it with fatha on both. From ʿIsa also: with damma on both. The Kufans recited iḥsanan. It was said: wa-wassayna is taken to imply "alzamna" (We obligated), which is transitive to two objects, so ḥusnan and iḥsanan are in the accusative as the second object of wa-wassayna. It was also said the meaning is: an enjoining of one who is good, or of one who does good. It is possible that ḥusnan means iḥsan, in which case it is an object of purpose, meaning: We enjoined him concerning them out of Our kindness to them, so the kindness is from Allah, exalted is He. It was also said the accusative is an infinitive (maṣdar) by making wa-wassayna imply "aḥsanna" (We did good), by enjoining upon man concerning his parents an act of kindness. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: and the accusative of this, meaning iḥsanan, is a plain infinitive and the second object of the genitive term, and the bāʾ is connected to wa-wassayna or to his saying iḥsanan. End of quote. It is not correct that it is connected to iḥsanan, because it is preceded by a verbal particle of the infinitive, and so its complement cannot precede it. Also, aḥsana is not transitive by the bāʾ; it is transitive by the lām. You say "aḥsantu li-Zaydin" (I did good to Zayd), and you do not say "aḥsantu bi-Zaydin," in the sense that the kindness reaches him. The discussion of ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 8] has preceded in surah al-ʿAnkabut, and it has been brought here with the discussion of that, as an additional benefit.

﴿His mother carried him with hardship﴾: the hardship is not at the beginning of her conception, but in the continuation of the pregnancy, since she has no control over carrying him or leaving him. End of quote. It is not that hardship befalls her at that time, so this is a remote possibility. Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the meaning is that she carried him with difficulty and gave birth to him with difficulty. The majority recited kurhan with a damma on the kaf. Shayba, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, the two Haramis (Makkan and Madinan) and Abu ʿAmr recited it with fatha. Abu Raja', Mujahid and ʿIsa recited it with both. The damma and fatha are two dialects with one meaning, like al-ʿaqr and al-ʿuqr. A group said: with damma it means hardship, and with fatha it means compulsion and coercion. They weakened the fatha recitation. Some said: if it were with fatha, she would have to be forced against herself, since its meaning is coercion and overpowering. End of quote. This is nothing, since the fatha recitation is in the seven mutawatir (widely transmitted) readings. Abu Hatim said: the recitation with fatha on the kaf is not good, because kurh with fatha means compulsion and overpowering. End of quote. Abu Hatim used to criticize some of the Qur'an with what he had no knowledge of, out of audacity on his part, may Allah pardon him. Their being in the accusative as states from the subject pronoun means: she carried him in a state of hardship, or it is an adjective of an omitted infinitive, meaning: a carrying that is hard.

﴿And his carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾: that is, the period of his carrying and weaning. This can only be if one of the two ends is shortened, either by the woman giving birth after six months and nursing for two years, or by her giving birth after nine months according to custom and nursing for two years minus a quarter of a year. If the gestation period increases, the period of nursing decreases. So the nursing period is one year and nine months, and completing the two years is for whoever wishes to complete the nursing. Experience has revealed that the minimum gestation period is six months, as the text of the Qur'an states. Galen said: I investigated diligently the usual duration of pregnancy, and I saw a woman who gave birth after one hundred and eighty-four nights. Ibn Sina claimed that he witnessed this. As for the maximum length of pregnancy, there is nothing in the Qur'an that indicates it. Ibn Sina said in al-Shifa': It reached me from someone I trust completely that a woman gave birth after the fourth year of pregnancy, and the child she bore had teeth growing. It is related from Aristotle that he said: the gestation period for every animal is fixed except for man, so it may happen that a child is born after seven months or eight, and rarely does the child survive in the eighth month, except in certain lands such as Egypt. End of quote. He expressed nursing by "fisal" (weaning) because nursing follows weaning and is connected to it, since it ends with it and is completed by it, so it was named after it. The majority recited wa-fisaluhu, which is the verbal noun of fasala, as if it is from two parties: he separated from his mother and she separated from him. Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Jahdari recited wa-faslahu. It was said that fasl and fisal are both verbal nouns, like fatm and fitam (weaning). Here is a subtle point: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the mother three times in His saying "to his parents," and in carrying him and nursing him, which is expressed by weaning, and He mentioned the father once in His saying "to his parents." This accords with what the Messenger said about making three-quarters of righteousness for the mother and one-quarter for the father: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, who deserves my goodness most?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your father.'"

﴿Until, when he reaches his maturity﴾: there is an omission in the speech, which would be: "until" as a limit for it, its estimated meaning: then he lived after that, or his life continued. The discussion of ﴿reaches his maturity﴾ has preceded in surah Yusuf. The apparent meaning is that the view of the one who says that reaching maturity is forty is weak, because of the conjunction ﴿and reaches forty years﴾. Conjunction requires difference, unless it is claimed that this is an emphasis on reaching maturity, in which case it is possible; but establishing a new meaning is preferable to emphasis. Reaching forty is the completion of reason, since the signs of success appear. It was said: no prophet was sent except after forty. It is said in a hadith: "Indeed, Satan drags his hand over the face of one who exceeds forty and does not repent, and says: 'By my father, a face that will not prosper!'"

﴿He said: "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that pleases You﴾: The discussion of this has preceded in surah al-Naml.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 46, verse 11–19 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And make my offspring righteous for me﴾: He asked that his offspring be made a place for righteousness and a likely source of it, as if he had said: "Grant me righteousness in my offspring," and so He placed it in them. Or it is implied (dammana): "And be kind to me in my offspring" (wa-ṭuff bī fī dhurriyyatī), because aṣlaḥ (to make righteous) takes a direct object by itself, as in His saying: ﴿And We made righteous for him his wife﴾ [al-Anbiya': 90]; therefore the phrase ﴿in my offspring﴾ needed interpretation. It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), and it extends to those after him. This is problematic, because it was revealed in Mecca, and his father embraced Islam in the year of the Conquest. And as for His saying: ﴿Those are they from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾: by this is not meant Abu Bakr or anyone else. The intended sense of "man" (al-insan) is the species, and therefore He indicated with His saying "those" (ulā'ika) in the plural. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yutaqabbalu" in the passive voice, with "aḥsanu" in the nominative, and likewise "wa-yatajawwazu"; Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Abu Ja'far, and al-A'mash (with a variant from him) read thus too. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read "nataqabbalu" with "aḥsana" in the accusative, and "natajawwazu" with the nun in both; al-Hasan, al-A'mash, and 'Isa read with the ya' in both, fathah, and "aḥsana" in the accusative.

﴿Among the companions of the Garden﴾: it was said that fi (in) here means ma'a (with). It was also said that it is like your saying: "The Amir honored me among a group of his companions," meaning among the total of those he honored from among them. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), in the sense of "being among the companions of the Garden." The phrase ﴿a true promise﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the preceding sentence, because His saying ﴿Those are they whom We accept﴾ is a promise from Him, may He be exalted, of acceptance and forgiveness. When He mentioned the person who was dutiful to his parents and what good resulted for him, He mentioned the one who was undutiful to his parents and what evil resulted for him. The intended sense of "those who" (alladhī) is the species, and therefore the predicate came in the plural in His saying: ﴿Those are they against whom the Word has come into effect﴾. Al-Hasan said: it refers to the disbelieving, undutiful son who denies resurrection. As for the saying of Marwan ibn al-Hakam, followed by Qatadah, that it was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, it is an erroneous statement arising from injustice, when Marwan, who was governor of Madinah, called for the allegiance to Yazid. 'Abd al-Rahman said: "Have you made it Heraclian (Hirqliyyah)? Whenever Heraclius dies, his son succeeds, and whenever Caesar dies, his son succeeds?" Marwan said: "Seize him!" So he entered the house of his sister 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), and 'A'ishah denied that. She said, and she was the one of truthful report (al-mastudaqah): "No verse of the Qur'an was revealed concerning the family of Abu Bakr except my innocence." She said: "By Allah, it is not about him, and if I wished to name him, I would have named him." She turned Marwan away and said: "But Allah cursed your father while you were in his loins, so you are a fragment (fadaḍ) of the curse of Allah." What proves the corruption of this statement is that He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Those are they against whom the Word has come into effect﴾, and these are the attributes of the disbelievers, the people of the Fire; and 'Abd al-Rahman was among the most excellent of the Companions, their chiefs and their heroes, and among those who had a notable contribution to Islam on the Day of Yamamah and other occasions.

﴿Uff to you both﴾: The discussion of uff, its meaning, dialects, and reading has preceded in Surah al-Isra'. The lam in "lakumā" is for explanation, i.e., for you both, I mean the expression of annoyance (ta'fif). The majority read ﴿Do you promise me﴾ with two nuns, the first kasrah; al-Hasan, 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr, and in one narration Hisham, read with the assimilation of the nun of the nominative into the nun of protection (nūn al-wiqāyah). Nafi' in one narration and a group read with a single nun. al-Hasan, Shaybah, and Abu Ja'far, with a variant from him, and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr, and Harun ibn Musa from al-Jahdari, and Sam from Hisham read with fathah on the first nun, as if they fled from the two kasrahs and the ya' toward fathah seeking lightness, so they made it fathah, just as the one who assimilates and the one who deletes fled. Abu Hatim said: fathah on the nun is false, an error.

(That I be brought forth): i.e., that I be brought out from my grave for resurrection and reckoning. The majority read "an ukhraja" in the passive voice, while al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, al-A'mash, Ibn Musarrif, and al-Dahhak read it in the active voice.

﴿And generations had passed away before me﴾: i.e., they had passed on, and none of them was brought out or resurrected. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: ﴿And generations had passed away before me﴾ denying resurrection.

﴿While both of them call upon Allah for help﴾: it is said: istaghath Allah and istaghath bi-Allah, and both usages are in the Arabic language. We have already refuted Ibn Malik's denial of its transitivity with the bā', and we mentioned evidence for that in al-Anfal. That is, they say: "Help (al-ghiyath) is with Allah from you and from your saying," and it is an exaggeration of his statement.

﴿Woe to you﴾: an invocation against him for destruction, and what is meant by it is urging and encouraging toward faith, not the literal reality of perdition. It was said: woe to you is said to one who is belittled and provoked toward a matter he is hastening toward. The Arab reader al-A'raj and 'Amr ibn Fa'idah read ﴿That the promise of Allah﴾ with fathah on the hamzah, i.e., "believe that the promise of Allah is true"; the majority read it with kasrah. ﴿And he says: "What is this?"﴾: i.e., what is this that he says? i.e., about the promise of resurrection from graves, "is nothing but tales of the ancients, which they wrote down in their books," and there is no reality to it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent sense of the words of this verse is that it was revealed concerning a specific individual who was spoken to and said such things, and Allah refuted his statements as a warning against falling into their like.
