The lam in "lakumā" is for explanation, i.e., for you both, I mean the expression of annoyance (ta'fif). The majority read ﴿Do you promise me﴾ with two nuns, the first kasrah; al-Hasan, 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr, and in one narration Hisham, read with the assimilation of the nun of the nominative into the nun of protection (nūn al-wiqāyah). Nafi' in one narration and a group read with a single nun. al-Hasan, Shaybah, and Abu Ja'far, with a variant from him, and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr, and Harun ibn Musa from al-Jahdari, and Sam from Hisham read with fathah on the first nun, as if they fled from the two kasrahs and the ya' toward fathah seeking lightness, so they made it fathah, just as the one who assimilates and the one who deletes fled. Abu Hatim said: fathah on the nun is false, an error.

(That I be brought forth): i.e., that I be brought out from my grave for resurrection and reckoning. The majority read "an ukhraja" in the passive voice, while al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, al-A'mash, Ibn Musarrif, and al-Dahhak read it in the active voice.

﴿And generations had passed away before me﴾: i.e., they had passed on, and none of them was brought out or resurrected. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: ﴿And generations had passed away before me﴾ denying resurrection.

﴿While both of them call upon Allah for help﴾: it is said: istaghath Allah and istaghath bi-Allah, and both usages are in the Arabic language. We have already refuted Ibn Malik's denial of its transitivity with the bā', and we mentioned evidence for that in al-Anfal. That is, they say: "Help (al-ghiyath) is with Allah from you and from your saying," and it is an exaggeration of his statement.

﴿Woe to you﴾: an invocation against him for destruction, and what is meant by it is urging and encouraging toward faith, not the literal reality of perdition. It was said: woe to you is said to one who is belittled and provoked toward a matter he is hastening toward. The Arab reader al-A'raj and 'Amr ibn Fa'idah read ﴿That the promise of Allah﴾ with fathah on the hamzah, i.e., "believe that the promise of Allah is true"; the majority read it with kasrah. ﴿And he says: "What is this?"﴾: i.e., what is this that he says? i.e., about the promise of resurrection from graves, "is nothing but tales of the ancients, which they wrote down in their books," and there is no reality to it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent sense of the words of this verse is that it was revealed concerning a specific individual who was spoken to and said such things, and Allah refuted his statements as a warning against falling into their like.

His saying "those" (ulā'ika), its apparent sense is that it is an indication of a species included in His saying "and the one who says," and it is possible that the verse concerns a specific individual, and His saying "those" would mean the category and species of this mentioned one: ﴿those against whom the Word has come into effect﴾, i.e., the word of Allah that He will punish them, ﴿among nations that had passed away before them of jinn and men﴾, meaning the totality of nations. This indicates that the jinn die generation after generation like men. al-Hasan said in one of his gatherings: the jinn do not die; Qatadah objected to him with this verse, and he fell silent. al-'Abbas, from Abu 'Amr, read ﴿that they were﴾ with fathah on the hamzah, and the majority with kasrah.

﴿And for each are degrees﴾: i.e., of the good-doer and the evil-doer, ﴿degrees﴾ — the term "degrees" (darajat) predominates, since Paradise consists of degrees (darajat) and the Fire of levels (darakat). The meaning: ranks and stations of reward for what they did of good and evil, and because of what they did of them. Ibn Zayd said: the degrees of the good-doers ascend upward, and the degrees of the evil-doers descend downward. End. The one providing the reason is omitted; its estimate is: "and that He may fully pay them their deeds in the measure of their recompense," so reward was made degrees and punishment was made levels. The majority read ﴿and that He may fully pay them﴾ with the ya', i.e., Allah, may He be exalted; al-A'mash, al-A'raj, Shaybah, Abu Ja'far, the two brothers, Ibn Dhakwan, and Nafi' (with a variant from him) read it with the nun; and al-Sulami read it with the ta' from above, i.e., "and We will fully pay them the degrees," attributing the fulfillment to them metaphorically.

(p-63) ﴿Wa-yawma yu'radu﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 34]: meaning, they will be tormented with the Fire, as one says, "He was exposed to the sword," when he was killed by it. And *al-'ard* (exposure) means direct contact, as you say, "I exposed the stick to the fire," meaning I brought the fire into direct contact with it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that what is meant is the exposure of the Fire to them, from their saying, 'I exposed the she-camel to the watering trough,' meaning they exposed the trough to her, and so they inverted the phrase. Ibn 'Abbas's explanation supports this: they will be brought to it, and it will be uncovered for them." End of quote. But the Qur'an should not be interpreted through inversion (*qalb*), since the correct view on inversion is that it is something resorted to only in poetry. When the meaning is sound and clear without inversion, what necessity calls for it? There is nothing in their saying, "I exposed the she-camel to the trough," nor in Ibn 'Abbas's explanation, that indicates inversion, because exposing the she-camel to the trough and exposing the trough to the she-camel are both valid, since *al-'ard* is a relative matter that can validly be ascribed to either the she-camel or the trough.

The majority of readers recited *adhhabtum* (you have squandered) as a statement, meaning it will be said to them: "You have squandered," and for this reason the *fa'* (then) in His words ﴿fa-al-yawma tujzawna﴾ (so today you will be recompensed) is apt. Qatadah, Mujahid, Ibn Waththab, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj and Ibn Kathir read it with a hamzah followed by an elongated vowel; Ibn 'Amir read it with two hamzahs, the first realized by Ibn Dhakwan, and the second softened by Hisham and Ibn Kathir in one transmission. From Hisham there is also a separation between the realized and the softened hamzah by an *alif*. This interrogative is meant as rebuke and affirmation, so it is in meaning a statement, and that is why the *fa'* is apt. Had it been a pure interrogative, the *fa'* would not have entered.

*Al-tayyibat* here means the pleasurable things: foods, drinks, clothing, bedding, mounts, paths, and other things enjoyed by people of luxury.

This verse exhorts people to minimize worldly life, to abandon indulgence in it, and to adopt asceticism and to be content with what sustains life. From the Messenger of God (ﷺ) there is in this what calls for emulating him. From 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) there are reports on this matter indicating his knowledge of the varieties of pleasures and the dignity of his soul that is above them: "Do you think we do not know the comfort of living? If I wished, I could have made for myself livers, roasted meats, *sifar* and *sala'iq*. But I preserve my good deeds, for God, Mighty and Majestic, described some people and said: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them﴾." *Al-sila'* is roasted meat; *al-sifar* is a condiment made of mustard and raisins; *al-sala'iq* is wide thin bread. Ibn 'Abbas said: "This is from the category of asceticism. Otherwise, the verse was revealed about the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the meaning is: good things of the Hereafter would have been yours had you believed, but you did not believe, so you hastened to your good things in the worldly life." This is then a metaphor for not believing, and for this reason the following was revealed about him: ﴿So today you will be recompensed with the torment of humiliation﴾. Had the outward meaning been intended, and it had not been a metaphor for what we have mentioned, the recompense with torment would not follow from it. It is also read *al-hawan* (humiliation), and both *al-hawan* and *al-hun* have the same meaning. Then He clarified this metaphor with His words: ﴿because you used to be arrogant﴾, meaning you held yourselves above faith; ﴿and because you used to transgress﴾, meaning through sins of the limbs. He placed the sin of the heart, which is arrogance, before the sins of the limbs, since the actions of the limbs arise from the intention of the heart.

Since the people of Makkah were absorbed in the pleasures of this world, turning away from faith and from what the Messenger brought, He reminded them of what happened to the earlier Arabs, namely the people of 'Ad. They had greater wealth, greater strength, and greater standing among their people, yet He imposed torment upon them because of their disbelief. He struck parables, and the stories of those who came before are known for exposing the ugliness of a thing and making it appear fair. So He said to His Messenger: Recount to your people, the people of Makkah, [the story of] Hud, peace be upon him, ﴿when he warned his people﴾, [the people of] 'Ad, whom God tormented ﴿in al-Ahqaf﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: a valley between 'Uman and Mahrah. Ibn Ishaq said: from 'Uman to (p-64) Hadramawt. Ibn Zayd said: sand dunes shining with light at al-Shihr in Yemen. It was also said: between Mahrah and 'Adan. Qatadah said: it is the lands of al-Shihr adjoining the Yemeni Sea. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is a mountain in Syria. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the correct view is that the land of 'Ad was in Yemen, and for them was ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ [al-Fajr: 7]. In the mention of this story there is a lesson for Quraysh and consolation for the Messenger, since his people denied him, just as 'Ad denied Hud, peace be upon him.

The clause in His words ﴿and warnings had passed before him and after him﴾: *al-nudhur* is the plural of *nadhir* (warner). The phrase ﴿min bayni yadayhi wa-min khalfihi﴾ (before him and after him) may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of "warnings," meaning the messengers who preceded his time are "before him," and those who were in his time are "after him." In this case, "after him" means after his warning. It is also possible that it is a parenthetical insertion between the warning of his people and "that you should not worship." The meaning is: those messengers who preceded him warned, and those who came after him did likewise, so mention them.

﴿They said: Have you come to us﴾: an interrogative of affirmation, rebuke, and challenge to him concerning what he warned them of, namely the great torment, for abandoning the singling out of God in worship.

﴿to turn us away﴾: to divert us, said al-Dahhak; or to remove us from our gods by falsehood, which is lying, meaning from the worship of our gods. ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾: a demand from them for the arrival of what he had promised them of torment. Do you not see His words: ﴿Nay, it is what you were hastening﴾?

﴿He said: Knowledge is only with God﴾: meaning the knowledge of the time of its arrival; the appointing of its time is not up to me, and I am only a conveyer of what God sent me with to you. When the promise of God was certain to him, and that it would befall them while they were heedless of it and denying, he said: ﴿But I see you as a people who are ignorant﴾: meaning you have no awareness of the outcome of your affair, and that is certainly going to happen.

'Ad had been withheld from rain by God for days, so God drove toward them a black cloud which came out at them from a valley called al-Mughith, and they rejoiced. The pronoun in ﴿when they saw it﴾: the apparent reading is that it refers to what is in "what you threaten us with," which is the torment, and *'aridan* (as a cloud) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the object. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may refer to the visible thing that appeared over them, which was explained by His words: ﴿as a cloud﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿When they saw it﴾: the pronoun has two possibilities: that it refers to what you threaten us with, or that it is ambiguous, its matter having been clarified by the word ﴿as a cloud﴾, which is either a specification (*tamyiz*) or a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and this is the more grammatically correct and eloquent." End of quote. What he claims to be the more grammatical and eloquent does not follow the rules the grammarians have stated, because the ambiguous pronoun that is explained and clarified by a specification occurs only with *rubba* (many a), as in "many a man I met," and with *ni'ma* and *bi'sa* (excellent and wretched) according to the view of the Basrans, as in "excellent is Zayd as a man" and "wretched is 'Amr as a youth." As for a circumstantial clause clarifying and explaining an ambiguous pronoun, we know of no one who held this view, and the grammarians have restricted the pronoun that is explained by what follows it, and they did not mention the object of "saw" when it is a pronoun, nor that a circumstantial clause explains and clarifies a pronoun.

*Al-'arid* is the cloud that stretches across the sky, bearing rain. From this is the poet's saying:

"O you who saw a cloud, for which I stayed awake, between the two forelegs and forehead of a lion."

And al-A'sha said:

"O you who saw a cloud, I have spent the night watching it, as though its lightning in its edges were flames."

﴿Facing their valleys﴾: this is the plural of *wadi* (valley), and the form *af'ilah* is the plural pattern for *fa'il*. This noun is irregular, like *nadin* and *andiyah*, and *ja'iz* and *ajwizah*. *Al-jA'iz* is the beam that stretches along the top of the roof. The annexation of "facing" (*mustaqbil*) and "raining" (*mumtirun*) is an annexation that does not confer definiteness, so for that reason the indefinite noun is qualified by them.

﴿Nay, it is what you were hastening﴾: meaning He said to them: it is that, that is, rather it is the torment you were hastening for. He turned away from their saying: ﴿This is a cloud bringing rain to us﴾, and informed that the torment had struck them suddenly. Then He said: ﴿a wind﴾: meaning it is a wind, a substitute (*badal*) for "it." He read *ma ist'ajaltum* with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *jim*. The stories about the wind have already been mentioned earlier, so there is no need to mention them here.

﴿Destroying﴾: meaning it annihilates. *Al-dammar* is destruction, which has already been mentioned. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *tadmur* with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, a *sukun* on the *dal*, and a *damma* on the *mim*. It was also read thus except with a *ya'* and with *kullu* in the nominative, meaning "everything is destroyed." "Everything" is a general term with a particular restriction, meaning from among their souls and their wealth, or from among what it was commanded to destroy. (p-65) The annexation of "Lord" to "wind" indicates that it and its directing are among the things that testify to His exalted power, for it is among the wonders of His creation and the greatest of His armies. He mentioned the command because it is commanded by Him, exalted is He. The majority read *la tura* with the second-person *ta'* ("you do not see") and *illa masakinahum* (except their dwellings) in the accusative; 'Abdullah, Mujahid, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Qatadah, Abu Hayyah, Talhah, 'Isa, al-Hasan, and 'Amr ibn Maymun, with one report from each of two of them, and 'Asim and Hamzah read *la yura* with a *ya'* prefix and a *damma*, "none is seen except their dwellings," in the nominative. Abu Raja' and Malik ibn Dinar, with one report from each: likewise. Al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and al-Sulami read it with a *ta'* prefix and a *damma*, "their dwellings" in the nominative. This is not permitted by our companions except in poetry, though some permit it in speech. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"As though it were a camel of sorrow, and nothing remained except the bones of the chest, the boards, and the sinews."

Another said:

"Nothing remained except the ribs, panting."

Isa al-Hamdani read *la yura* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, "none is seen except its dwelling," in the singular. This was also reported from al-A'mash and Nasr ibn 'Asim. It was also read *la tara* with an open *ta'* for the second person, "you do not see except its dwelling," in the singular and accusative. The plural was dispensed with in favour of the singular to diminish their status, and because when they perished at one time, it was as though they had been in one dwelling.

When He had informed of the destruction of the people of 'Ad, He addressed Quraysh by way of admonition, saying: ﴿And We had established them﴾ [the earlier verse in full: "And We had indeed established them in that in which We have not established you"]. *In* here is negative, meaning: in that in which We did not establish them, namely strength, wealth, and expansiveness of bodies and possessions. The negation was not expressed with the word *ma* out of dislike for repeating the same word, even though the meaning differs. It was also said: *in* is conditional, with its answer omitted, and the implied meaning is: "if We had established you in it, you would have transgressed." It was also said: *in* is superfluous after the relative *ma*, made similar to the negative *ma* and the temporal *ma*, so in the verse it is like in the saying:

"A man hopes for what he does not see, while calamities stand between him and what is nearest to him."

That is, We established them in the same condition in which We established you. Taking ما as a negative particle (نافية) is the preferred reading, because the Qur'an points to this in several places, such as His saying: ﴿They were more numerous than them, and stronger in power and in monuments﴾ [Ghafir 40:82], and His saying: ﴿They are better in furnishings and in appearance﴾ [Maryam 19:74]. This reading is also more forceful in reproach and more effective in urging reflection (i'tibar).

Then he enumerated His blessings upon them, and showed that these did not avail them anything, since they did not use the hearing, the sight and the hearts for what they ought to have been used for.

It has been said that ما is interrogative in the sense of affirmation (taqrir, a question that compels the listener to affirm). But this is remote, as in His saying (مِن شَيْءٍ), because the sense would become: "Which of the things mentioned availed them anything?" In that case مِن would be an extra particle (zā'ida) in an affirmative clause (mūjab), and that is not permissible according to the sound view. The governing element of إذ is أغنى.

The sense of causation (ta'līl) appears in إذ if you say: "I honored Zayd for his kindness to me," or "when he was kind to me." The two are equal in time, and what is understood from إذ is what is understood from the causal lām. Your honoring him at the time of his kindness to you was only because his kindness to you existed at that time.

(p-63) ﴿Wa-yawma yu'radu﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 34]: meaning, they will be tormented with the Fire, as one says, "He was exposed to the sword," when he was killed by it. And *al-'ard* (exposure) means direct contact, as you say, "I exposed the stick to the fire," meaning I brought the fire into direct contact with it. It was also said: between Mahrah and 'Adan. Qatadah said: it is the lands of al-Shihr adjoining the Yemeni Sea. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is a mountain in Syria. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the correct view is that the land of 'Ad was in Yemen, and for them was ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ [al-Fajr: 7]. The clause in His words ﴿and warnings had passed before him and after him﴾: *al-nudhur* is the plural of *nadhir* (warner). The phrase ﴿min bayni yadayhi wa-min khalfihi﴾ (before him and after him) may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of "warnings," meaning the messengers who preceded his time are "before him," and those who were in his time are "after him." In this case, "after him" means after his warning. It is also possible that it is a parenthetical insertion between the warning of his people and "that you should not worship." The meaning is: those messengers who preceded him warned, and those who came after him did likewise, so mention them.

﴿They said: Have you come to us﴾: an interrogative of affirmation, rebuke, and challenge to him concerning what he warned them of, namely the great torment, for abandoning the singling out of God in worship.

﴿to turn us away﴾: to divert us, said al-Dahhak; or to remove us from our gods by falsehood, which is lying, meaning from the worship of our gods. ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾: a demand from them for the arrival of what he had promised them of torment. 'Ad had been withheld from rain by God for days, so God drove toward them a black cloud which came out at them from a valley called al-Mughith, and they rejoiced. *Al-'arid* is the cloud that stretches across the sky, bearing rain. From this is the poet's saying:

"O you who saw a cloud, for which I stayed awake, between the two forelegs and forehead of a lion."

And al-A'sha said:

"O you who saw a cloud, I have spent the night watching it, as though its lightning in its edges were flames."

In that case مِن would be an extra particle (zā'ida) in an affirmative clause (mūjab), and that is not permissible according to the sound view. The governing element of إذ is أغنى.

The sense of causation (ta'līl) appears in إذ if you say: "I honored Zayd for his kindness to me," or "when he was kind to me." The two are equal in time, and what is understood from إذ is what is understood from the causal lām. Your honoring him at the time of his kindness to you was only because his kindness to you existed at that time.

(p-66)﴿And We destroyed the towns around you, and We varied the signs so that they might return.﴾ ﴿Why then did those whom they had taken as gods besides God, as means of drawing near, not help them? Rather, they went astray from them. That was their falsehood, and what they used to fabricate.﴾ ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of jinn listening to the Qur'an. When they were present, they said, "Be silent." And when it was finished, they returned to their people as warners.﴾ ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path.﴾ ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of God and believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Whoever does not respond to the caller of God cannot escape on earth, and he has no protectors besides Him. Those are in manifest error.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, indeed; He is over all things powerful.﴾ ﴿On the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ ﴿So be patient as the steadfast messengers were patient, and do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them. On the Day they see what they are promised, it will seem to them that they stayed only an hour of a day. [This is] a proclamation. Will anyone be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾.

﴿And We destroyed the towns around you﴾: This is an address to the Quraysh, by way of making an example of them. Those towns around them were Ma'rib, Hijr, Thamud and Sodom. He means by the people of the towns: ﴿and We varied the signs﴾, that is, the proofs, the evidences and the admonitions for the people of those towns, (so that they might return) from what they were in of disbelief to belief, but they did not return.

﴿Why then did [they] not help them﴾: that is, why did they not help them when destruction came upon them? (Those who took): that is, took them, ﴿besides God as means of drawing near﴾: that is, in the state of seeking nearness and making them intercessors. (Gods): this is the second object of "took," and the first is the omitted pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun. Al-Hawfi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' allowed that "as means of drawing near" be the second object of "took," with "gods" being a substitute for it (badal). Al-Zamakhshari said: "And 'as means of drawing near' is a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and it is not valid that it be the second object with 'gods' as a substitute for it, because of the corruption of the meaning." End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari did not explain how the meaning is corrupted, and it appears that the meaning is sound according to that grammatical analysis (i'rab). Al-Hawfi also allowed that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi).

﴿Rather, they went astray from them﴾: that is, they were absent from helping them. The majority read ﴿ifkuhum﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, a sukun on the fa' and a damma on the kaf, and Ibn 'Abbas in one narration [read it] with a fatha on the hamza. "Ifk" is a verbal noun (masdar) of the form "ifk." Ibn 'Abbas also read, as did Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Sabbah ibn al-'Ala' al-Ansari, Abu 'Iyad, Ikrima, Hanzala ibn al-Nu'man ibn Murra and Mujahid: ﴿afakahum﴾ with three fathas, meaning he turned them away. Abu 'Iyad and Ikrima likewise [read it so], except that they doubled the fa' for intensification, and Ibn al-Zubayr also, and Ibn 'Abbas, according to what Ibn Khalawayh reported: ﴿a'fakahum﴾ with a long vowel, which may be a form of "faʿala" (to do to one another), with the hamza being original, or a form of "af'ala" (causative), with the hamza marking transitivity, meaning he made them turn away (ya'fikun), and "af'ala" here has the sense of the basic form. It is reported from al-Farra' that it was read ﴿afakuhum﴾ with a fatha on the hamza and the fa' and a damma on the kaf, which is a dialect form of "ifk." Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by Qutrub and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, [read] ﴿afikuhum﴾ as an active participle from "afaka," meaning he turned them away. The reference of "that" for whoever read ﴿ifkuhum﴾ as a verbal noun is to the taking of idols as gods, meaning: that is their lying and fabrication. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And 'that' is an indication of the impossibility of their gods helping them and their going astray from them, meaning: that is the effect of their falsehood, which is their taking them as gods, and the fruit of their polytheism and their fabrication of lies against God, [in claiming] that He has partners." End of quote. According to the reading of whoever made it a verb, its meaning is: that taking [of gods] turned them away from the truth, and likewise the reading of the active participle, meaning it turned them away from the truth. It is possible that "ma" be a verbal (masdar) particle, meaning "and their fabrication," and that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which), with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning they fabricate it.

﴿And when We turned towards you a group of jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾: The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when He had shown that the human is believer and disbeliever, and mentioned that the jinn too include believers and disbelievers, and this came after the story of Hud and his people, because of the severity and strength of his people. The jinn are also described with that, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿An 'ifrit from the jinn said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place, and indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it."﴾ [al-Naml: 39]. What the people of Hud were destroyed by was the wind, and it is from the realm which is not seen; only its blowing is perceived. The jinn are also from the realm which is not seen. Hud, upon him be peace, was from the Arabs, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was from the Arabs, so this may be a connection to this verse with what comes before it. In it there is also a rebuke to the Quraysh and the disbelieving Arabs, since this Book, the miraculous one, was sent down to them, and they disbelieved in it, although they are people of the language in which the Qur'an was revealed and of the same kind as the Messenger who was sent to them. These [jinn] are jinn, so they are not of his kind, yet the hearing of the Qur'an affected them, and they believed in it and in the one to whom it was revealed, and they knew that it was from God, unlike the Quraysh and their likes, who persist in disbelieving in it.

﴿And when We turned﴾: directed towards you. He [some] read ﴿sarrafna﴾ with a doubled ra' because they were a group, so the intensification is according to the situation.

﴿A group of jinn﴾: "nafar" is fewer than ten and its plural is "anfar." Ibn 'Abbas said: they were seven, among them Zawba'a. What reconciles the differing narrations is that the story of the jinn occurred twice.

The first: when he returned from al-Ta'if, having gone out to them seeking their support, in an episode mentioned by the authors of the biographies (sira). It is narrated that the jinn used to eavesdrop, but when the Messenger was sent, the heaven was guarded and the jinn were struck with shooting stars. They said: "This is nothing but that something has happened." They roamed the earth and came upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at Wadi Nakhla, while he was standing praying, and they listened to his recitation without his knowing, so God informed him of their listening.

The second time: God commanded him to warn the jinn and recite to them, and he said: "I have been commanded to recite to the jinn, so whoever will follow me?" He said it three times, and they lowered their heads except 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. He said: No one attended the night of the jinn except me. We set off until, when we were at the ravine of al-Hajun, he drew a line for me and said: "Do not leave it until I return to you." Then he began the Qur'an. I heard a great commotion until I feared for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and many dark shapes covered him between me and him, so that I could not hear his voice. Then they dispersed like clouds. He said to me: "Did you see anything?" I said: "Yes, men, black, with white garments tucked up." He said: "Those were the jinn of Nasibin," and they were twelve thousand. The surah he recited to them was ﹛Read in the name of your Lord﹜ [al-'Alaq: 1]. At the end of this hadith I said: "O Messenger of God, I heard a commotion from them." He said: "They were disputing over a slain man of theirs, and I judged with the truth." It has been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that "no one attended the night of the jinn," and God knows best the soundness of that.

﴿When they were present﴾: that is, the Qur'an, meaning they were within earshot of it. It was also said: they were present before the Messenger. This is a shift (iltifat) from "to you" to the third-person pronoun.

﴿They said, "Be silent"﴾: that is, be quiet in order to listen. In it is an instruction to attend while learning, and how one should learn. The majority read ﴿qudiya﴾ in the passive form. Abu Mijlaz and Habib ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr read ﴿qada﴾ in the active form, meaning Muhammad completed what he recited, that is, finished it and concluded it. Ibn 'Umar and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: he recited to them the surah of al-Rahman, and whenever he said ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 16], they said: "None of Your blessings do we deny, our Lord, to You be praise."

﴿They returned to their people as warners﴾: they dispersed to the lands warning the jinn. Qatada said: "How quickly the people understood!" End of quote. At that point occurred the story of Sawad ibn Qarib and Khunafir and their likes, when their companions from the jinn came to them, and that was the cause of their conversion to Islam.

﴿After Moses﴾: that is, after the Book of Moses. 'Ata' said: they were upon the creed of the Jews. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the jinn had not heard of the matter of Jesus. This is not sound from Ibn 'Abbas. How could they not have heard of the matter of Jesus when he has a great community that is not limited to his creed? So it is far-fetched that the jinn did not hear of him. It is possible that they said ﴿after Moses﴾ as an alert to their people to follow the Messenger, since Moses had given good news of him, so they said that this matter is mentioned in the Torah, ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ from the Torah, the Gospel and the divine Books, since they all include tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood, the return (ma'ad), and the command to purify morals.

﴿Guiding to the truth﴾: that is, to what is true in itself and sincere, which is known by clear reason. (And to a straight path): he varied between the two expressions, and the meaning is close, and sometimes one of them is used where the other is not used, so he combined them here and the repetition is good.

﴿Respond to the caller of God﴾: he is the Messenger, and the intermediary who conveys from Him. ﴿O our people, respond﴾: refers to God.

﴿He will forgive you some of your sins﴾: "min" here is partitive (lil-tab'id), because belief does not forgive wrongs done to others. Al-Zamakhshari said this meaning. It was also said: "min" is extra (za'ida), because Islam wipes out what came before it, so no liability remains with it.

﴿And protect you from a painful punishment﴾: all of this and the apparent meanings of the Qur'an indicate reward, and likewise Ibn 'Abbas said: they have reward and they have punishment; they meet in Paradise and crowd at its gates. It was also said: there is no reward for them except deliverance from the Fire, and Abu Hanifa used to hold this view.

﴿Cannot escape on earth﴾: that is, he cannot escape from His punishment, since there is no refuge from it and no place to flee, like His saying: ﴿And we thought that we would not escape God on earth, nor could we escape Him by flight﴾ [al-Jinn: 12]. It is reported from Ibn 'Amir: ﴿wa-laysa lahum﴾ with an added mim. The majority read ﴿wa-lam ya'ya﴾, the imperfect of "ʿayiya" on the pattern "fa'ila" with a kasra on the ʿayn; al-Hasan read ﴿wa-lam ya'i﴾ with a kasra on the ʿayn and a sukun on the ya'. Its explanation is that in the perfect the ʿayn of the root was given a fatha, as they said of "baqiya": "baqa," and this is a dialect of Tayy. When the perfect was built on "fa'ila" with a fatha on the ʿayn, its imperfect was built on "yaf'ilu" with a kasra on the ʿayn, so it came as "ya'ya." When the jussive particle entered, it dropped the ya', so "ya'ya" remained with the vowel of the ya' transferred to the ʿayn, so the ya' became quiescent and it remained "ya'i." The majority read ﴿bi-qadir﴾ as an active participle, and the bi' is extra in the predicate of "inna," and what precedes it being in the sphere of negation made the addition of it good. Al-Zajjaj allowed: "Ma zanantu anna ahadan bi-qa'im" (I did not think that anyone was standing), by analogy with this, but the correct view is to limit that to what is heard (samaʿ, i.e., attested usage). So it is as if in the verse he said: "Is God not able?" Do you not see how He brought "bala" (yes indeed) confirming the giving of life to the dead, not their seeing? ﴿Al-Jahdari, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, 'Isa, al-A'raj (with a variant from him) and Ya'qub﴾ read ﴿yuqaddir﴾ as an imperfect verb.

﴿Is this not the truth?﴾: that is, it will be said to them, and the reference of "this" is to the punishment, meaning: you used to deny that you would be punished. The meaning is a rebuke for their mockery of God's promise and threat and their saying: ﴿And we will not be punished﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 138].

﴿They said, "Yes, by our Lord."﴾ This is affirmation at a time when it no longer benefits them. Al-Hasan said: They will be punished in the Fire while they are content with it for their own souls, acknowledging that it is justice. Then the one answering them from among the angels will say at that point: (So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve. So be patient, as the steadfast messengers (ulu al-ʿazm) were patient.) The fa' here is conjunctive, linking this sentence to the preceding sentence about the state of the disbelievers in the Hereafter, and the meaning between them is connected: that is their condition with God. So do not hasten, and be patient, and fear none but God. Ulu al-ʿazm means the people of resolve among the messengers, those who were known for steadfastness with their people and for striving. So min here is partitive (lil-tabʿid). It has been said that it may also be explanatory (lil-bayan), meaning those who are the messengers, so that all the messengers would be ulu al-ʿazm. Taking min as partitive implies that some of them were messengers and some were not messengers, while taking it as explanatory implies that they are the messengers. The partitive reading is the view of ʿAta al-Khurasani and al-Kalbi, and the explanatory reading is the view of Ibn Zayd. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: They are the eighteen mentioned in Surat al-Anʿam, because God said after mentioning them: (So follow their guidance). Muqatil said: They are six: Noah, who was patient for a long time with the harm of his people; Abraham, who was patient with the fire; Isaac, who submitted himself to slaughter; Jacob, who was patient over the loss of his son and the blindness of his sight, and said (so patience is fitting); Joseph, who was patient with prison and the well; and Job, who was patient with affliction. Others added: Moses, whose people said: (Indeed we are overtaken) [al-Shuʿara 61], (He said: No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me) [al-Shuʿara 62]; David, who wept over his sin for forty years; and Jesus, who did not place one brick upon another and said: "It is a crossing, so cross it, and do not build it up."

﴿And do not hasten [the punishment] for them﴾: that is, for the disbelievers of Quraysh. Do not ask God to hasten it for them, for it will certainly descend upon them, even if it is delayed. At that time they will consider the period they remained in this world to be short, as if (they had not remained but an hour). Ubayy recited: min al-nahar (from the day). The majority recited: min nahar (of a day). The majority recited: balaghun (a message/sufficiency), with a nominative ending, and the apparent reference is to the period in which they remained, as if it were said: that hour is their balagh, just as He said, Exalted is He: (a brief enjoyment). So balaghun is the predicate of an omitted subject. It has been said that balaghun may mean the Qur'an and the Law, that is, this is a message, meaning a conveying and a warning. Abu Mijlaz said: balaghun is the subject and its predicate is lahum (for them), and one stops at "So do not hasten." This is not good, because it separates parts of the speech from one another, since the apparent meaning of his statement "for them" is that it is connected to his statement "So do not hasten for them." The intervening element is the similitude clause between the predicate and the subject. al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, and ʿIsa recited: balaghan, with the accusative ending. This allows that the meaning is: a message in the Qur'an, that is, they were conveyed a message, or we conveyed a message. Al-Hasan also recited: balaghin, with the genitive ending, as an adjective of nahar. Abu Mijlaz and Abu Sarah al-Hudhali recited: "ʿAli conveyed the matter to the Prophet (ﷺ)," and this supports taking balaghun, in both the nominative and accusative readings, to mean the conveying of the Qur'an and the Law. Also from Abu Mijlaz: ballagha as a past-tense verb. The majority recited: yuhlaku, with a dammah on the yaʾ and a fatḥah on the lam. Ibn Muhaysin, as transmitted from him by Ibn Khalawayh, recited it with a fatḥah on the yaʾ and a kasrah on the lam. Also from him: with a fatḥah on both the yaʾ and the lam, and its past tense is halaka with a kasrah on the lam, which is a dialectal form. Abu al-Fath said: it is a form that is disliked. Zayd ibn Thabit recited: yuhlik, with a dammah on the yaʾ and a kasrah on the lam.

﴿Except the defiantly disobedient people﴾: in the accusative. In this verse there is a threat and a warning.

﴿When they were present﴾: that is, the Qur'an, meaning they were within earshot of it. It was also said: they were present before the Messenger. This is a shift (iltifat) from "to you" to the third-person pronoun.

﴿They said, "Be silent"﴾: that is, be quiet in order to listen. In it is an instruction to attend while learning, and how one should learn. The majority read ﴿qudiya﴾ in the passive form. Abu Mijlaz and Habib ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr read ﴿qada﴾ in the active form, meaning Muhammad completed what he recited, that is, finished it and concluded it. Ibn 'Umar and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: he recited to them the surah of al-Rahman, and whenever he said ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 16], they said: "None of Your blessings do we deny, our Lord, to You be praise."

﴿They returned to their people as warners﴾: they dispersed to the lands warning the jinn. Qatada said: "How quickly the people understood!" End of quote. At that point occurred the story of Sawad ibn Qarib and Khunafir and their likes, when their companions from the jinn came to them, and that was the cause of their conversion to Islam.

﴿After Moses﴾: that is, after the Book of Moses. 'Ata' said: they were upon the creed of the Jews. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the jinn had not heard of the matter of Jesus. This is not sound from Ibn 'Abbas. How could they not have heard of the matter of Jesus when he has a great community that is not limited to his creed? So it is far-fetched that the jinn did not hear of him. It is possible that they said ﴿after Moses﴾ as an alert to their people to follow the Messenger, since Moses had given good news of him, so they said that this matter is mentioned in the Torah, ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ from the Torah, the Gospel and the divine Books, since they all include tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood, the return (ma'ad), and the command to purify morals.

﴿Guiding to the truth﴾: that is, to what is true in itself and sincere, which is known by clear reason. (And to a straight path): he varied between the two expressions, and the meaning is close, and sometimes one of them is used where the other is not used, so he combined them here and the repetition is good.

﴿Respond to the caller of God﴾: he is the Messenger, and the intermediary who conveys from Him. ﴿O our people, respond﴾: refers to God.

﴿He will forgive you some of your sins﴾: "min" here is partitive (lil-tab'id), because belief does not forgive wrongs done to others. Al-Zamakhshari said this meaning. It was also said: "min" is extra (za'ida), because Islam wipes out what came before it, so no liability remains with it.

﴿And protect you from a painful punishment﴾: all of this and the apparent meanings of the Qur'an indicate reward, and likewise Ibn 'Abbas said: they have reward and they have punishment; they meet in Paradise and crowd at its gates. It was also said: there is no reward for them except deliverance from the Fire, and Abu Hanifa used to hold this view.

﴿Cannot escape on earth﴾: that is, he cannot escape from His punishment, since there is no refuge from it and no place to flee, like His saying: ﴿And we thought that we would not escape God on earth, nor could we escape Him by flight﴾ [al-Jinn: 12]. It is reported from Ibn 'Amir: ﴿wa-laysa lahum﴾ with an added mim. The majority read ﴿wa-lam ya'ya﴾, the imperfect of "ʿayiya" on the pattern "fa'ila" with a kasra on the ʿayn; al-Hasan read ﴿wa-lam ya'i﴾ with a kasra on the ʿayn and a sukun on the ya'. Its explanation is that in the perfect the ʿayn of the root was given a fatha, as they said of "baqiya": "baqa," and this is a dialect of Tayy. When the perfect was built on "fa'ila" with a fatha on the ʿayn, its imperfect was built on "yaf'ilu" with a kasra on the ʿayn, so it came as "ya'ya." When the jussive particle entered, it dropped the ya', so "ya'ya" remained with the vowel of the ya' transferred to the ʿayn, so the ya' became quiescent and it remained "ya'i." The majority read ﴿bi-qadir﴾ as an active participle, and the bi' is extra in the predicate of "inna," and what precedes it being in the sphere of negation made the addition of it good. Al-Zajjaj allowed: "Ma zanantu anna ahadan bi-qa'im" (I did not think that anyone was standing), by analogy with this, but the correct view is to limit that to what is heard (samaʿ, i.e., attested usage). So it is as if in the verse he said: "Is God not able?" Do you not see how He brought "bala" (yes indeed) confirming the giving of life to the dead, not their seeing? ﴿Al-Jahdari, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, 'Isa, al-A'raj (with a variant from him) and Ya'qub﴾ read ﴿yuqaddir﴾ as an imperfect verb.

﴿Is this not the truth?﴾: that is, it will be said to them, and the reference of "this" is to the punishment, meaning: you used to deny that you would be punished. The meaning is a rebuke for their mockery of God's promise and threat and their saying: ﴿And we will not be punished﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 138].

﴿They said, "Yes, by our Lord."﴾ This is affirmation at a time when it no longer benefits them. Al-Hasan said: They will be punished in the Fire while they are content with it for their own souls, acknowledging that it is justice. Then the one answering them from among the angels will say at that point: (So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve. So be patient, as the steadfast messengers (ulu al-ʿazm) were patient.) The fa' here is conjunctive, linking this sentence to the preceding sentence about the state of the disbelievers in the Hereafter, and the meaning between them is connected: that is their condition with God. So do not hasten, and be patient, and fear none but God. Ulu al-ʿazm means the people of resolve among the messengers, those who were known for steadfastness with their people and for striving. So min here is partitive (lil-tabʿid). It has been said that it may also be explanatory (lil-bayan), meaning those who are the messengers, so that all the messengers would be ulu al-ʿazm. Taking min as partitive implies that some of them were messengers and some were not messengers, while taking it as explanatory implies that they are the messengers. The partitive reading is the view of ʿAta al-Khurasani and al-Kalbi, and the explanatory reading is the view of Ibn Zayd. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: They are the eighteen mentioned in Surat al-Anʿam, because God said after mentioning them: (So follow their guidance). Muqatil said: They are six: Noah, who was patient for a long time with the harm of his people; Abraham, who was patient with the fire; Isaac, who submitted himself to slaughter; Jacob, who was patient over the loss of his son and the blindness of his sight, and said (so patience is fitting); Joseph, who was patient with prison and the well; and Job, who was patient with affliction. Others added: Moses, whose people said: (Indeed we are overtaken) [al-Shuʿara 61], (He said: No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me) [al-Shuʿara 62]; David, who wept over his sin for forty years; and Jesus, who did not place one brick upon another and said: "It is a crossing, so cross it, and do not build it up."

﴿And do not hasten [the punishment] for them﴾: that is, for the disbelievers of Quraysh. Do not ask God to hasten it for them, for it will certainly descend upon them, even if it is delayed. At that time they will consider the period they remained in this world to be short, as if (they had not remained but an hour). Ubayy recited: min al-nahar (from the day). The majority recited: min nahar (of a day). The majority recited: balaghun (a message/sufficiency), with a nominative ending, and the apparent reference is to the period in which they remained, as if it were said: that hour is their balagh, just as He said, Exalted is He: (a brief enjoyment). So balaghun is the predicate of an omitted subject. It has been said that balaghun may mean the Qur'an and the Law, that is, this is a message, meaning a conveying and a warning. Abu Mijlaz said: balaghun is the subject and its predicate is lahum (for them), and one stops at "So do not hasten." This is not good, because it separates parts of the speech from one another, since the apparent meaning of his statement "for them" is that it is connected to his statement "So do not hasten for them." The intervening element is the similitude clause between the predicate and the subject. al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, and ʿIsa recited: balaghan, with the accusative ending. This allows that the meaning is: a message in the Qur'an, that is, they were conveyed a message, or we conveyed a message. Al-Hasan also recited: balaghin, with the genitive ending, as an adjective of nahar. Abu Mijlaz and Abu Sarah al-Hudhali recited: "ʿAli conveyed the matter to the Prophet (ﷺ)," and this supports taking balaghun, in both the nominative and accusative readings, to mean the conveying of the Qur'an and the Law. Also from Abu Mijlaz: ballagha as a past-tense verb. The majority recited: yuhlaku, with a dammah on the yaʾ and a fatḥah on the lam. Ibn Muhaysin, as transmitted from him by Ibn Khalawayh, recited it with a fatḥah on the yaʾ and a kasrah on the lam. Also from him: with a fatḥah on both the yaʾ and the lam, and its past tense is halaka with a kasrah on the lam, which is a dialectal form. Abu al-Fath said: it is a form that is disliked. Zayd ibn Thabit recited: yuhlik, with a dammah on the yaʾ and a kasrah on the lam.

﴿Except the defiantly disobedient people﴾: in the accusative. In this verse there is a threat and a warning.

(p-66)﴿And We destroyed the towns around you, and We varied the signs so that they might return.﴾ ﴿Why then did those whom they had taken as gods besides God, as means of drawing near, not help them? Rather, they went astray from them. That was their falsehood, and what they used to fabricate.﴾ ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of jinn listening to the Qur'an. When they were present, they said, "Be silent." And when it was finished, they returned to their people as warners.﴾ ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path.﴾ ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of God and believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Whoever does not respond to the caller of God cannot escape on earth, and he has no protectors besides Him. Those are in manifest error.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, indeed; He is over all things powerful.﴾ ﴿On the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ ﴿So be patient as the steadfast messengers were patient, and do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them. On the Day they see what they are promised, it will seem to them that they stayed only an hour of a day. [This is] a proclamation. Will anyone be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾.

﴿And We destroyed the towns around you﴾: This is an address to the Quraysh, by way of making an example of them. Those towns around them were Ma'rib, Hijr, Thamud and Sodom. He means by the people of the towns: ﴿and We varied the signs﴾, that is, the proofs, the evidences and the admonitions for the people of those towns, (so that they might return) from what they were in of disbelief to belief, but they did not return.

﴿Why then did [they] not help them﴾: that is, why did they not help them when destruction came upon them? (Those who took): that is, took them, ﴿besides God as means of drawing near﴾: that is, in the state of seeking nearness and making them intercessors. (Gods): this is the second object of "took," and the first is the omitted pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun. Al-Hawfi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' allowed that "as means of drawing near" be the second object of "took," with "gods" being a substitute for it (badal). Al-Zamakhshari said: "And 'as means of drawing near' is a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and it is not valid that it be the second object with 'gods' as a substitute for it, because of the corruption of the meaning." End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari did not explain how the meaning is corrupted, and it appears that the meaning is sound according to that grammatical analysis (i'rab). Al-Hawfi also allowed that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi).

﴿Rather, they went astray from them﴾: that is, they were absent from helping them. The majority read ﴿ifkuhum﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, a sukun on the fa' and a damma on the kaf, and Ibn 'Abbas in one narration [read it] with a fatha on the hamza. "Ifk" is a verbal noun (masdar) of the form "ifk." Ibn 'Abbas also read, as did Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Sabbah ibn al-'Ala' al-Ansari, Abu 'Iyad, Ikrima, Hanzala ibn al-Nu'man ibn Murra and Mujahid: ﴿afakahum﴾ with three fathas, meaning he turned them away. Abu 'Iyad and Ikrima likewise [read it so], except that they doubled the fa' for intensification, and Ibn al-Zubayr also, and Ibn 'Abbas, according to what Ibn Khalawayh reported: ﴿a'fakahum﴾ with a long vowel, which may be a form of "faʿala" (to do to one another), with the hamza being original, or a form of "af'ala" (causative), with the hamza marking transitivity, meaning he made them turn away (ya'fikun), and "af'ala" here has the sense of the basic form. It is reported from al-Farra' that it was read ﴿afakuhum﴾ with a fatha on the hamza and the fa' and a damma on the kaf, which is a dialect form of "ifk." Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by Qutrub and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, [read] ﴿afikuhum﴾ as an active participle from "afaka," meaning he turned them away. The reference of "that" for whoever read ﴿ifkuhum﴾ as a verbal noun is to the taking of idols as gods, meaning: that is their lying and fabrication. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And 'that' is an indication of the impossibility of their gods helping them and their going astray from them, meaning: that is the effect of their falsehood, which is their taking them as gods, and the fruit of their polytheism and their fabrication of lies against God, [in claiming] that He has partners." End of quote. According to the reading of whoever made it a verb, its meaning is: that taking [of gods] turned them away from the truth, and likewise the reading of the active participle, meaning it turned them away from the truth. It is possible that "ma" be a verbal (masdar) particle, meaning "and their fabrication," and that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which), with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning they fabricate it.

﴿And when We turned towards you a group of jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾: The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when He had shown that the human is believer and disbeliever, and mentioned that the jinn too include believers and disbelievers, and this came after the story of Hud and his people, because of the severity and strength of his people. The jinn are also described with that, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿An 'ifrit from the jinn said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place, and indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it."﴾ [al-Naml: 39]. What the people of Hud were destroyed by was the wind, and it is from the realm which is not seen; only its blowing is perceived. The jinn are also from the realm which is not seen. Hud, upon him be peace, was from the Arabs, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was from the Arabs, so this may be a connection to this verse with what comes before it. In it there is also a rebuke to the Quraysh and the disbelieving Arabs, since this Book, the miraculous one, was sent down to them, and they disbelieved in it, although they are people of the language in which the Qur'an was revealed and of the same kind as the Messenger who was sent to them. These [jinn] are jinn, so they are not of his kind, yet the hearing of the Qur'an affected them, and they believed in it and in the one to whom it was revealed, and they knew that it was from God, unlike the Quraysh and their likes, who persist in disbelieving in it.

﴿And when We turned﴾: directed towards you. He [some] read ﴿sarrafna﴾ with a doubled ra' because they were a group, so the intensification is according to the situation.

﴿A group of jinn﴾: "nafar" is fewer than ten and its plural is "anfar." Ibn 'Abbas said: they were seven, among them Zawba'a. What reconciles the differing narrations is that the story of the jinn occurred twice.

The first: when he returned from al-Ta'if, having gone out to them seeking their support, in an episode mentioned by the authors of the biographies (sira). It is narrated that the jinn used to eavesdrop, but when the Messenger was sent, the heaven was guarded and the jinn were struck with shooting stars. They said: "This is nothing but that something has happened." They roamed the earth and came upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at Wadi Nakhla, while he was standing praying, and they listened to his recitation without his knowing, so God informed him of their listening.

The second time: God commanded him to warn the jinn and recite to them, and he said: "I have been commanded to recite to the jinn, so whoever will follow me?" He said it three times, and they lowered their heads except 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. He said: No one attended the night of the jinn except me. We set off until, when we were at the ravine of al-Hajun, he drew a line for me and said: "Do not leave it until I return to you." Then he began the Qur'an. I heard a great commotion until I feared for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and many dark shapes covered him between me and him, so that I could not hear his voice. Then they dispersed like clouds. He said to me: "Did you see anything?" I said: "Yes, men, black, with white garments tucked up." He said: "Those were the jinn of Nasibin," and they were twelve thousand. The surah he recited to them was ﹛Read in the name of your Lord﹜ [al-'Alaq: 1]. At the end of this hadith I said: "O Messenger of God, I heard a commotion from them." He said: "They were disputing over a slain man of theirs, and I judged with the truth." It has been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that "no one attended the night of the jinn," and God knows best the soundness of that.

Also from him: with a fatḥah on both the yaʾ and the lam, and its past tense is halaka with a kasrah on the lam, which is a dialectal form. Abu al-Fath said: it is a form that is disliked. Zayd ibn Thabit recited: yuhlik, with a dammah on the yaʾ and a kasrah on the lam.

﴿Except the defiantly disobedient people﴾: in the accusative. In this verse there is a threat and a warning.

(p-66)﴿And We destroyed the towns around you, and We varied the signs so that they might return.﴾ ﴿Why then did those whom they had taken as gods besides God, as means of drawing near, not help them? Rather, they went astray from them. That was their falsehood, and what they used to fabricate.﴾ ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of jinn listening to the Qur'an. When they were present, they said, "Be silent." And when it was finished, they returned to their people as warners.﴾ ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path.﴾ ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of God and believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Whoever does not respond to the caller of God cannot escape on earth, and he has no protectors besides Him. Those are in manifest error.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, indeed; He is over all things powerful.﴾ ﴿On the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ ﴿So be patient as the steadfast messengers were patient, and do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them. On the Day they see what they are promised, it will seem to them that they stayed only an hour of a day. [This is] a proclamation. Will anyone be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾.

﴿And We destroyed the towns around you﴾: This is an address to the Quraysh, by way of making an example of them. Those towns around them were Ma'rib, Hijr, Thamud and Sodom. He means by the people of the towns: ﴿and We varied the signs﴾, that is, the proofs, the evidences and the admonitions for the people of those towns, (so that they might return) from what they were in of disbelief to belief, but they did not return.

﴿Why then did [they] not help them﴾: that is, why did they not help them when destruction came upon them? (Those who took): that is, took them, ﴿besides God as means of drawing near﴾: that is, in the state of seeking nearness and making them intercessors. (Gods): this is the second object of "took," and the first is the omitted pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun. Al-Hawfi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' allowed that "as means of drawing near" be the second object of "took," with "gods" being a substitute for it (badal). Al-Zamakhshari said: "And 'as means of drawing near' is a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and it is not valid that it be the second object with 'gods' as a substitute for it, because of the corruption of the meaning." End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari did not explain how the meaning is corrupted, and it appears that the meaning is sound according to that grammatical analysis (i'rab). Al-Hawfi also allowed that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi).

﴿Rather, they went astray from them﴾: that is, they were absent from helping them. The majority read ﴿ifkuhum﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, a sukun on the fa' and a damma on the kaf, and Ibn 'Abbas in one narration [read it] with a fatha on the hamza. "Ifk" is a verbal noun (masdar) of the form "ifk." Ibn 'Abbas also read, as did Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Sabbah ibn al-'Ala' al-Ansari, Abu 'Iyad, Ikrima, Hanzala ibn al-Nu'man ibn Murra and Mujahid: ﴿afakahum﴾ with three fathas, meaning he turned them away. Abu 'Iyad and Ikrima likewise [read it so], except that they doubled the fa' for intensification, and Ibn al-Zubayr also, and Ibn 'Abbas, according to what Ibn Khalawayh reported: ﴿a'fakahum﴾ with a long vowel, which may be a form of "faʿala" (to do to one another), with the hamza being original, or a form of "af'ala" (causative), with the hamza marking transitivity, meaning he made them turn away (ya'fikun), and "af'ala" here has the sense of the basic form. It is reported from al-Farra' that it was read ﴿afakuhum﴾ with a fatha on the hamza and the fa' and a damma on the kaf, which is a dialect form of "ifk." Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by Qutrub and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, [read] ﴿afikuhum﴾ as an active participle from "afaka," meaning he turned them away. The reference of "that" for whoever read ﴿ifkuhum﴾ as a verbal noun is to the taking of idols as gods, meaning: that is their lying and fabrication. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And 'that' is an indication of the impossibility of their gods helping them and their going astray from them, meaning: that is the effect of their falsehood, which is their taking them as gods, and the fruit of their polytheism and their fabrication of lies against God, [in claiming] that He has partners." End of quote. According to the reading of whoever made it a verb, its meaning is: that taking [of gods] turned them away from the truth, and likewise the reading of the active participle, meaning it turned them away from the truth. It is possible that "ma" be a verbal (masdar) particle, meaning "and their fabrication," and that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which), with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning they fabricate it.

﴿And when We turned towards you a group of jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾: The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when He had shown that the human is believer and disbeliever, and mentioned that the jinn too include believers and disbelievers, and this came after the story of Hud and his people, because of the severity and strength of his people. The jinn are also described with that, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿An 'ifrit from the jinn said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place, and indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it."﴾ [al-Naml: 39]. What the people of Hud were destroyed by was the wind, and it is from the realm which is not seen; only its blowing is perceived. The jinn are also from the realm which is not seen. Hud, upon him be peace, was from the Arabs, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was from the Arabs, so this may be a connection to this verse with what comes before it. In it there is also a rebuke to the Quraysh and the disbelieving Arabs, since this Book, the miraculous one, was sent down to them, and they disbelieved in it, although they are people of the language in which the Qur'an was revealed and of the same kind as the Messenger who was sent to them. These [jinn] are jinn, so they are not of his kind, yet the hearing of the Qur'an affected them, and they believed in it and in the one to whom it was revealed, and they knew that it was from God, unlike the Quraysh and their likes, who persist in disbelieving in it.

﴿And when We turned﴾: directed towards you. He [some] read ﴿sarrafna﴾ with a doubled ra' because they were a group, so the intensification is according to the situation.

﴿A group of jinn﴾: "nafar" is fewer than ten and its plural is "anfar." Ibn 'Abbas said: they were seven, among them Zawba'a. What reconciles the differing narrations is that the story of the jinn occurred twice.

The first: when he returned from al-Ta'if, having gone out to them seeking their support, in an episode mentioned by the authors of the biographies (sira). It is narrated that the jinn used to eavesdrop, but when the Messenger was sent, the heaven was guarded and the jinn were struck with shooting stars. They said: "This is nothing but that something has happened." They roamed the earth and came upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at Wadi Nakhla, while he was standing praying, and they listened to his recitation without his knowing, so God informed him of their listening.

The second time: God commanded him to warn the jinn and recite to them, and he said: "I have been commanded to recite to the jinn, so whoever will follow me?" He said it three times, and they lowered their heads except 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. He said: No one attended the night of the jinn except me. We set off until, when we were at the ravine of al-Hajun, he drew a line for me and said: "Do not leave it until I return to you." Then he began the Qur'an. I heard a great commotion until I feared for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and many dark shapes covered him between me and him, so that I could not hear his voice. Then they dispersed like clouds. He said to me: "Did you see anything?" I said: "Yes, men, black, with white garments tucked up." He said: "Those were the jinn of Nasibin," and they were twelve thousand. The surah he recited to them was ﹛Read in the name of your Lord﹜ [al-'Alaq: 1]. At the end of this hadith I said: "O Messenger of God, I heard a commotion from them." He said: "They were disputing over a slain man of theirs, and I judged with the truth." It has been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that "no one attended the night of the jinn," and God knows best the soundness of that.

﴿When they were present﴾: that is, the Qur'an, meaning they were within earshot of it. It was also said: they were present before the Messenger. This is a shift (iltifat) from "to you" to the third-person pronoun.

﴿They said, "Be silent"﴾: that is, be quiet in order to listen. In it is an instruction to attend while learning, and how one should learn. The majority read ﴿qudiya﴾ in the passive form. Abu Mijlaz and Habib ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr read ﴿qada﴾ in the active form, meaning Muhammad completed what he recited, that is, finished it and concluded it. Ibn 'Umar and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: he recited to them the surah of al-Rahman, and whenever he said ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 16], they said: "None of Your blessings do we deny, our Lord, to You be praise."

﴿They returned to their people as warners﴾: they dispersed to the lands warning the jinn. Qatada said: "How quickly the people understood!" End of quote. At that point occurred the story of Sawad ibn Qarib and Khunafir and their likes, when their companions from the jinn came to them, and that was the cause of their conversion to Islam.

﴿After Moses﴾: that is, after the Book of Moses. 'Ata' said: they were upon the creed of the Jews. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the jinn had not heard of the matter of Jesus. This is not sound from Ibn 'Abbas. How could they not have heard of the matter of Jesus when he has a great community that is not limited to his creed? So it is far-fetched that the jinn did not hear of him. It is possible that they said ﴿after Moses﴾ as an alert to their people to follow the Messenger, since Moses had given good news of him, so they said that this matter is mentioned in the Torah, ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ from the Torah, the Gospel and the divine Books, since they all include tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood, the return (ma'ad), and the command to purify morals.

﴿Guiding to the truth﴾: that is, to what is true in itself and sincere, which is known by clear reason. (And to a straight path): he varied between the two expressions, and the meaning is close, and sometimes one of them is used where the other is not used, so he combined them here and the repetition is good.

﴿Respond to the caller of God﴾: he is the Messenger, and the intermediary who conveys from Him. ﴿O our people, respond﴾: refers to God.

﴿He will forgive you some of your sins﴾: "min" here is partitive (lil-tab'id), because belief does not forgive wrongs done to others. Al-Zamakhshari said this meaning. It was also said: "min" is extra (za'ida), because Islam wipes out what came before it, so no liability remains with it.

﴿And protect you from a painful punishment﴾: all of this and the apparent meanings of the Qur'an indicate reward, and likewise Ibn 'Abbas said: they have reward and they have punishment; they meet in Paradise and crowd at its gates. It was also said: there is no reward for them except deliverance from the Fire, and Abu Hanifa used to hold this view.

﴿Cannot escape on earth﴾: that is, he cannot escape from His punishment, since there is no refuge from it and no place to flee, like His saying: ﴿And we thought that we would not escape God on earth, nor could we escape Him by flight﴾ [al-Jinn: 12]. It is reported from Ibn 'Amir: ﴿wa-laysa lahum﴾ with an added mim. The majority read ﴿wa-lam ya'ya﴾, the imperfect of "ʿayiya" on the pattern "fa'ila" with a kasra on the ʿayn; al-Hasan read ﴿wa-lam ya'i﴾ with a kasra on the ʿayn and a sukun on the ya'. Its explanation is that in the perfect the ʿayn of the root was given a fatha, as they said of "baqiya": "baqa," and this is a dialect of Tayy. When the perfect was built on "fa'ila" with a fatha on the ʿayn, its imperfect was built on "yaf'ilu" with a kasra on the ʿayn, so it came as "ya'ya." When the jussive particle entered, it dropped the ya', so "ya'ya" remained with the vowel of the ya' transferred to the ʿayn, so the ya' became quiescent and it remained "ya'i." The majority read ﴿bi-qadir﴾ as an active participle, and the bi' is extra in the predicate of "inna," and what precedes it being in the sphere of negation made the addition of it good. Al-Zajjaj allowed: "Ma zanantu anna ahadan bi-qa'im" (I did not think that anyone was standing), by analogy with this, but the correct view is to limit that to what is heard (samaʿ, i.e., attested usage). So it is as if in the verse he said: "Is God not able?" Do you not see how He brought "bala" (yes indeed) confirming the giving of life to the dead, not their seeing? ﴿Al-Jahdari, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, 'Isa, al-A'raj (with a variant from him) and Ya'qub﴾ read ﴿yuqaddir﴾ as an imperfect verb.

﴿Is this not the truth?﴾: that is, it will be said to them, and the reference of "this" is to the punishment, meaning: you used to deny that you would be punished. The meaning is a rebuke for their mockery of God's promise and threat and their saying: ﴿And we will not be punished﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 138].

﴿They said, "Yes, by our Lord."﴾ This is affirmation at a time when it no longer benefits them. Al-Hasan said: They will be punished in the Fire while they are content with it for their own souls, acknowledging that it is justice. Then the one answering them from among the angels will say at that point: (So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve. So be patient, as the steadfast messengers (ulu al-ʿazm) were patient.) The fa' here is conjunctive, linking this sentence to the preceding sentence about the state of the disbelievers in the Hereafter, and the meaning between them is connected: that is their condition with God. So do not hasten, and be patient, and fear none but God. Ulu al-ʿazm means the people of resolve among the messengers, those who were known for steadfastness with their people and for striving. So min here is partitive (lil-tabʿid). It has been said that it may also be explanatory (lil-bayan), meaning those who are the messengers, so that all the messengers would be ulu al-ʿazm. Taking min as partitive implies that some of them were messengers and some were not messengers, while taking it as explanatory implies that they are the messengers. The partitive reading is the view of ʿAta al-Khurasani and al-Kalbi, and the explanatory reading is the view of Ibn Zayd. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: They are the eighteen mentioned in Surat al-Anʿam, because God said after mentioning them: (So follow their guidance). Muqatil said: They are six: Noah, who was patient for a long time with the harm of his people; Abraham, who was patient with the fire; Isaac, who submitted himself to slaughter; Jacob, who was patient over the loss of his son and the blindness of his sight, and said (so patience is fitting); Joseph, who was patient with prison and the well; and Job, who was patient with affliction. Others added: Moses, whose people said: (Indeed we are overtaken) [al-Shuʿara 61], (He said: No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me) [al-Shuʿara 62]; David, who wept over his sin for forty years; and Jesus, who did not place one brick upon another and said: "It is a crossing, so cross it, and do not build it up."

﴿And do not hasten [the punishment] for them﴾: that is, for the disbelievers of Quraysh. Do not ask God to hasten it for them, for it will certainly descend upon them, even if it is delayed. At that time they will consider the period they remained in this world to be short, as if (they had not remained but an hour). Ubayy recited: min al-nahar (from the day). The majority recited: min nahar (of a day). The majority recited: balaghun (a message/sufficiency), with a nominative ending, and the apparent reference is to the period in which they remained, as if it were said: that hour is their balagh, just as He said, Exalted is He: (a brief enjoyment). So balaghun is the predicate of an omitted subject. It has been said that balaghun may mean the Qur'an and the Law, that is, this is a message, meaning a conveying and a warning. Abu Mijlaz said: balaghun is the subject and its predicate is lahum (for them), and one stops at "So do not hasten." This is not good, because it separates parts of the speech from one another, since the apparent meaning of his statement "for them" is that it is connected to his statement "So do not hasten for them." The intervening element is the similitude clause between the predicate and the subject. al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, and ʿIsa recited: balaghan, with the accusative ending. This allows that the meaning is: a message in the Qur'an, that is, they were conveyed a message, or we conveyed a message. Al-Hasan also recited: balaghin, with the genitive ending, as an adjective of nahar.
